problem: Calibration and failure-detection research pools all errors, but errors near the decision boundary and errors far on the wrong side have different causes, signatures, and remedies; the pooled treatment produces mitigation methods that look better than they behave.
core_hypothesis: The error population of vision FMs is bimodal in confidence and in cause: high-confidence errors trace to shortcuts and priors while low-confidence errors trace to genuine ambiguity, and standard mitigations (temperature scaling, selective prediction, TTA) exclusively address the low-confidence mode, leaving the high-confidence mode as an invariant residual.
falsifiable_prediction: Cause-audited error sets will show confidence bimodality with cause enrichment per mode, and applying standard mitigations will reduce diffident errors substantially while the confident-error rate stays statistically unchanged across mitigation families.
why_important: The confident-error mode is the dangerous one in deployment; if standard tooling structurally cannot touch it, safety cases built on calibration and abstention are systematically overstated.
why_possibly_novel: Overconfidence is well known in aggregate; a two-population causal decomposition with a mitigation-invariance claim appears uncrystallized (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect errors for several classifiers/detectors, audit causes via counterfactual probes (context swap, texture randomization), test bimodality, apply mitigation families, and measure per-mode reduction.
main_risk: The confidence boundary between modes may be blurry and dataset-dependent, requiring the causal audit rather than a simple threshold to define populations.
community_default_belief: Better calibration plus selective prediction handles the practical error problem; error confidence is a continuum, not a mixture of mechanisms.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Shortcut activations produce evidence-like internal signals, so no recalibration of the same signal can flag them; the continuum view hides a mechanism boundary that mitigation cannot cross.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: histogram error confidences for one model on a shortcut-rich dataset, test for bimodality, and check temperature scaling's effect on the high-confidence lobe.

one_line: Per-pixel segmentation confidence is spatially anti-aligned with error severity: lowest at tolerable boundary zones, highest inside regions where errors are catastrophic whole-instance mistakes.
problem: Downstream systems consume segmentation confidence maps as risk maps, but confidence is trained per-pixel and concentrates uncertainty at boundaries, while the costly failures (mislabeling an entire region or instance) occur in high-confidence interiors.
core_hypothesis: The spatial distribution of segmentation confidence is dominated by boundary proximity rather than semantic risk, so severity-weighted risk (probability times cost of the error at that pixel) is anti-correlated with the confidence map's implied risk over a large fraction of images, making confidence maps actively misleading for downstream risk consumers.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets where errors can be classified by severity (boundary-offset versus wrong-region), the confidence map will rank boundary pixels as riskiest while realized severe errors concentrate in interior pixels ranked safe, yielding negative rank correlation between confidence-implied and severity-weighted realized risk.
why_important: Autonomous systems and medical pipelines gate decisions on segmentation confidence; a demonstrated anti-alignment would show that gating logic is pointed at the wrong pixels.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary-concentrated uncertainty is a known descriptive fact; the severity-weighted anti-alignment claim and its consequence for downstream gating appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several segmenters, decompose errors into boundary-offset and region-level classes with severity weights, compute realized-risk maps, and correlate with model confidence maps across images.
main_risk: Severity weighting is application-specific; results need at least two distinct downstream cost models to show robustness of the conclusion.
community_default_belief: Segmentation confidence maps are imperfect but directionally useful risk signals across the image.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Per-pixel cross-entropy training makes confidence a proxy for local label ambiguity, and label ambiguity is structurally highest at exactly the pixels where errors matter least.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: on a driving dataset, check whether whole-instance segmentation errors occur predominantly in the top confidence quartile of pixels.

one_line: Classification confidence and localization quality of detections are nearly statistically independent, so score-threshold failure mining systematically misses the well-scored badly-localized failure stratum.
problem: Failure mining and deployment gating both use the classification score as the master quality signal, implicitly assuming it also reflects localization quality, an assumption that decoupled training losses give no reason to support.
core_hypothesis: Across detector families, the mutual information between classification score and localization error (IoU with truth) is low, so a distinct failure stratum exists (high score, poor box) that score-based mining never samples, and this stratum is enriched in downstream-harmful cases (truncated boxes on pedestrians, merged boxes on adjacent objects).
falsifiable_prediction: Joint distributions of score and IoU will show near-independence beyond a weak trend, and audits of high-score detections will find localization failures at rates far exceeding what score-based failure models predict, with family-specific structure (set-prediction versus anchor-based differing in stratum shape).
why_important: If the miner cannot see a whole failure stratum, targeted improvement loops (mine, retrain, redeploy) converge to models that are precisely wrong: confident, plausible, badly localized.
why_possibly_novel: Localization-aware scoring papers exist as fixes; the failure-mining blind-spot framing with stratum enrichment analysis appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several public detectors, compute score-IoU joint statistics on standard benchmarks, quantify the high-score/low-IoU stratum, and audit its content composition against downstream harm categories.
main_risk: IoU-aware heads (already present in some detectors) may partially couple the variables, requiring family-stratified conclusions rather than a universal claim.
community_default_belief: Detection score is an adequate single quality signal; low-quality boxes mostly come with low scores.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Classification and regression branches optimize different losses on different targets, and nothing in standard training forces their errors to correlate; independence is the default outcome, not the exception.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: scatter-plot score versus IoU for one detector's true-positive-matched detections on COCO val and compute their correlation.

one_line: Calibration transfers across class-prior shift in a predictable direction: models calibrated on balanced sets become overconfident on majority classes and underconfident on minority classes in deployment, with error computable from the prior ratio alone.
problem: Calibration is fit on curated evaluation distributions and shipped into deployments with different class priors; the resulting miscalibration is treated as unpredictable drift rather than a computable, correctable quantity.
core_hypothesis: For softmax classifiers, deployment miscalibration under pure prior shift follows the analytic Bayes correction determined by the train-to-deploy prior ratio, so measured deployment calibration error will match the closed-form prediction, and applying the correction restores calibration without new labeled data beyond prior estimates.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructing deployment sets with controlled prior shifts will produce calibration error curves matching the analytic prediction across shift magnitudes, and prior-corrected models will show near-baseline calibration while uncorrected temperature scaling fails in the predicted direction.
why_important: Prior shift is the most common deployment shift and prior estimates are often available operationally; a validated closed-form fix would replace expensive recalibration cycles for a large class of deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Prior correction is classical for accuracy; its systematic validation as the dominant, predictable component of deployed FM miscalibration appears under-documented (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resample a benchmark into several prior-shifted deployment sets, measure calibration error of frozen models with and without analytic prior correction, and compare against the closed-form curve.
main_risk: Real deployment shifts mix prior shift with covariate shift, so the clean predictability claim applies to the prior component and needs a decomposition method in the wild.
community_default_belief: Deployment miscalibration is a symptom of general distribution shift requiring learned recalibration on deployment data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The prior-shift component of miscalibration is mathematically determined and needs no learning; treating it as unpredictable conflates the correctable part with the genuinely hard covariate part.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: resample CIFAR/ImageNet val to a skewed prior, measure a frozen model's calibration error, and compare against the analytic prediction.

one_line: Under style shift (paintings, sketches, renders), model confidence does not degrade smoothly but bifurcates toward extremes, invalidating threshold-based OOD triggers precisely on stylized inputs.
problem: OOD monitoring assumes confidence decreases with distribution distance, but style-shifted inputs may resolve to either strong-but-wrong prior matches or total feature mismatch, producing a bimodal rather than shifted confidence distribution.
core_hypothesis: As inputs move along a photo-to-abstract style continuum, per-input confidence distributions transition from unimodal to bimodal (near-one and near-zero lobes) rather than shifting downward, so any single confidence threshold either floods alerts or misses the confident-wrong lobe entirely.
falsifiable_prediction: Confidence histograms along a controlled stylization continuum will show growing bimodality (dip statistic increasing), and threshold-based OOD detectors will exhibit a characteristic precision-recall collapse at intermediate stylization that density-based detectors on features do not show.
why_important: Stylized and rendered content is ubiquitous in user-generated and synthetic-media streams; monitoring that structurally fails on this slice leaves a large deployment surface unguarded.
why_possibly_novel: Style robustness is measured in accuracy; the confidence-distribution-shape analysis and its consequence for threshold monitors appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate a stylization continuum for a fixed image set (style transfer at graded strengths), record confidence distributions for several classifiers, test for bimodality trends, and benchmark threshold versus density OOD detectors along the continuum.
main_risk: Stylization methods introduce content distortion correlated with strength, so content must be verified stable (human check) to attribute effects to style alone.
community_default_belief: Confidence declines roughly monotonically as inputs leave the training distribution, so thresholds trade sensitivity against alert volume smoothly.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Style shift does not move inputs uniformly away from all classes; it moves them toward whatever class's training data contained similar styles, creating confident capture rather than graceful decay.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: stylize 200 photos at five strengths, histogram a classifier's max-softmax per strength, and test for bimodality.

one_line: SAM-style mask quality scores inherit the prompt distribution of training: quality prediction fails specifically for atypical prompts (boundary-adjacent, off-center, multi-point), mis-ranking masks exactly when users prompt unusually.
problem: Promptable segmenters ship a learned quality head used to select among candidate masks, but that head was trained under a synthetic prompt distribution, and its reliability conditioned on prompt typicality is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Quality-score reliability (correlation with true IoU) degrades sharply as prompts depart from the training prompt distribution, so for boundary-adjacent or unusually-placed prompts the model both segments worse and mis-scores its candidates, compounding failure at selection time.
falsifiable_prediction: Binning interactions by prompt typicality (distance from object center, proximity to boundary, prompt count) will show quality-score-to-true-IoU correlation collapsing in atypical bins while remaining high in typical bins, and oracle selection among candidates will beat score-based selection by the largest margins exactly in the atypical bins.
why_important: Interactive segmentation workflows trust the score to auto-select masks at scale (dataset labeling, medical contouring); a prompt-conditional reliability hole silently corrupts downstream datasets where prompting is naturally atypical.
why_possibly_novel: SAM failure analyses focus on mask quality; conditional reliability analysis of the quality head under prompt-distribution shift appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample prompts across a typicality grid on a labeled dataset, record SAM candidate masks with scores and true IoUs, and estimate score-IoU correlation per bin plus oracle-versus-score selection gaps.
main_risk: Prompt typicality must be estimated relative to SAM's actual training prompt synthesis, which is only partially documented, so a proxy typicality model is needed.
community_default_belief: The predicted-IoU head is a reliable, roughly uniform quality signal across reasonable user prompts.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Learned quality heads are regressors valid on their training input distribution; prompt placement is an input to that regressor, and users explore regions synthetic prompt generation never covered.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: for 300 objects, compare score-IoU correlation between center-point prompts and near-boundary prompts.

one_line: A single temperature calibrated in-domain moves calibration in a predictable harmful direction under covariate shift (overconfidence grows with feature-space shift distance), making shift distance a sufficient statistic for recalibration.
problem: Temperature scaling is the default calibration fix, but its transfer behavior under shift is treated as unpredictable, though the direction (shifted inputs get relatively overconfident) may be systematic and quantifiable.
core_hypothesis: Calibration error under covariate shift grows monotonically with feature-space distance from the calibration set, always in the overconfident direction for in-domain-calibrated models, so a distance-conditioned temperature (one scalar function, no shift labels) restores most calibration across shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: Across shift benchmarks, plotting calibration error against mean feature distance will show a monotone overconfident trend for temperature-scaled models, and a distance-conditioned temperature fit on one shift family will transfer to unseen shift families with large calibration recovery.
why_important: It would replace per-domain recalibration with a single deployable rule, and provide a falsifiable structural law about how confidence degrades, useful for monitoring design.
why_possibly_novel: Accuracy-on-the-line style regularities exist for accuracy; a corresponding distance-law for calibration direction with a transferable conditional temperature appears unconsolidated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate temperature-scaled classifiers across corruption and natural-shift suites, regress signed calibration error on feature distance, fit the conditional temperature on half the shifts, and test transfer on the rest.
main_risk: Some shifts (label-correlated or adversarially structured) may break monotonicity, restricting the law to covariate-only shifts and requiring a shift-type detector.
community_default_belief: Calibration transfer under shift is idiosyncratic; each deployment domain needs its own recalibration data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Shift-induced overconfidence has a common mechanism (softmax saturation on off-manifold features), and common mechanisms produce lawful, not idiosyncratic, behavior.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: for one model on a corruption suite, plot signed calibration error versus corruption severity and check the monotone overconfident trend.

one_line: VLMs switch from vision to language-prior answering at a measurable visual-evidence threshold: a psychometric 'blindness point' that is a stable model constant across content.
problem: Language-prior bias in VLMs is documented anecdotally, but there is no quantitative model of when the switch happens, so failures look random rather than governed by an evidence-strength threshold.
core_hypothesis: For questions with prior-consistent and prior-violating answers, VLM accuracy as a function of visual evidence strength (contrast, size, occlusion of the deciding cue) follows a psychometric curve whose inflection (the blindness point) is stable across content domains for a given model, making prior-override behavior predictable from one calibration set.
falsifiable_prediction: Psychometric curves measured on one content domain will predict the evidence threshold at which the same model abandons visual evidence in other domains, and models ranked by blindness point on synthetic stimuli will retain that ranking on natural counterexample benchmarks.
why_important: A single-number characterization of prior dominance enables model selection and risk assessment for applications where images routinely contradict priors (defect detection, medical anomalies).
why_possibly_novel: Counterintuitive-image benchmarks exist; extracting a transferable psychometric constant for prior override appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build stimulus ladders degrading the visual cue that contradicts a strong prior (e.g., a green stop sign at graded visibility), fit psychometric curves per model per domain, and test cross-domain threshold stability.
main_risk: Evidence strength is multidimensional (size, contrast, blur), so the threshold may be cue-specific rather than a single constant, complicating but not invalidating the framework.
community_default_belief: Prior-driven errors are qualitative quirks to be trained away, not lawful threshold phenomena that can be measured and compared.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The switch reflects a quantitative competition between evidence and prior inside a fixed computation; fixed computations produce reproducible tradeoff curves, which is exactly what psychometrics measures.
fastest_falsification: One day: create one cue-degradation ladder for one counterintuitive scene family, query two VLMs, and check whether accuracy follows a sigmoid with model-specific thresholds.

one_line: VLM counting errors mirror human numerosity psychophysics (exact subitizing up to about four, logarithmic error growth beyond) because caption statistics encode human number usage, not because models perceive numerosity.
problem: Counting failures are reported as accuracy tables; the structure of the errors (which counts get confused with which) is unanalyzed, leaving the mechanism (perceptual limits versus linguistic priors) unresolved.
core_hypothesis: VLM count-response distributions will show human-like signatures: near-perfect small-number performance, scalar variability (error proportional to magnitude), and round-number attraction, and these signatures will track caption corpus number-word frequencies rather than image encoder capacity, implying counting is linguistic prior readout above the subitizing range.
falsifiable_prediction: Error distributions will show variance growing with true count and mass concentrated on round numbers matching corpus frequency, and interventions that change visual encoding capacity (resolution, crops) will not move the large-count error structure, while prompt phrasing that shifts linguistic framing will.
why_important: If counting is prior readout, applications needing counts (inventory, biology, crowd estimates) require structured decomposition tools rather than better VLM scaling, redirecting engineering effort.
why_possibly_novel: Counting weakness is well documented; the psychophysical signature analysis tied to caption statistics as the mechanism appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Query VLMs on controlled dot/object arrays across counts, fit variance-versus-magnitude and round-number attraction models, and compare against number-word frequencies from open caption corpora and against resolution-intervention controls.
main_risk: Tokenizer representation of numbers introduces its own artifacts that must be separated from corpus frequency effects.
community_default_belief: Counting failure is a visual grounding limitation that scale and resolution will progressively fix.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If failure were visual, error structure would track visual variables; the hypothesis predicts it tracks linguistic variables instead, which resolution cannot fix.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: query one VLM on arrays of 3 to 60 dots, histogram responses, and check for round-number spikes and scalar variance growth.

one_line: Left/right spatial-relation failures in VLMs are chiral: systematically asymmetric in a direction matching reading-order statistics of training captions, so mirroring images flips the error asymmetry.
problem: Spatial relation benchmarks report symmetric-looking accuracy numbers, but if errors are directionally biased by language statistics, the aggregate hides a chiral structure that mirroring would expose.
core_hypothesis: VLMs answer 'A left of B' questions with an asymmetric error profile (one direction systematically overreported), the asymmetry sign matches subject-first/reading-order biases in caption corpora, and horizontally mirroring the entire evaluation flips the model's error asymmetry, proving the bias is representational rather than stimulus-driven.
falsifiable_prediction: Signed error asymmetry will be significantly nonzero and consistent across content, will flip sign under global image mirroring, and will correlate across models with the reading-order statistics of their (documented) caption sources.
why_important: Chiral failure is invisible to standard accuracy but decisive for robotics and AR instructions where left/right correctness is the whole task; the mirroring test also provides a cheap audit tool for any deployed VLM.
why_possibly_novel: Spatial reasoning weakness is documented in aggregate; the chirality signature, mirror-flip causal test, and corpus-statistics linkage appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build balanced left/right scenes, measure signed asymmetry per model, rerun with mirrored images, and verify sign flip plus magnitude preservation.
main_risk: Object-category confounds (some objects appear more often on one side in photos) must be controlled by synthetic balance and per-pair counterbalancing.
community_default_belief: Spatial relation errors are symmetric noise from weak spatial grounding, equally likely in both directions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The text decoder generates relations with language-model priors that are directionally biased by reading order and phrase frequency; symmetric noise is the least likely outcome for a language-mediated readout.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 100 two-object scenes, ask left/right, mirror all images, re-ask, and compare signed error asymmetries.

one_line: Open-vocabulary detectors and VLMs match negated queries ('a cup without a handle') to the negated concept itself, and the failure is diagnosable entirely from the text encoder's geometry before any image is seen.
problem: Negation failures are typically evaluated end-to-end, mixing vision and language causes; if the text embedding of a negated phrase lands near the affirmative embedding, the system fails for a purely textual reason predictable offline.
core_hypothesis: For contrastive text encoders, embeddings of negated attribute phrases are dominated by the negated content word, so text-side similarity structure alone (negated phrase near affirmative phrase) predicts image-side failure rates per concept, and text-encoder-only audits can forecast which negation queries a deployment will get wrong without any image evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: Cosine similarity between negated and affirmative phrase embeddings will predict per-concept negation failure rates on image benchmarks with strong correlation, and interventions purely on the text side (compositional re-encoding) will recover image-task accuracy in proportion to the text-geometry fix.
why_important: Negation is common in safety-relevant queries (find products without safety caps); an offline text-side audit that forecasts failures cheaply changes how such systems are validated.
why_possibly_novel: Negation weakness in CLIP-like models is documented; the quantitative text-geometry-to-image-failure forecasting claim appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute negated-affirmative embedding similarities for a concept battery, evaluate open-vocab detection with negated queries on a labeled set, and regress failure rates on text-side similarity.
main_risk: Some negation failures may be genuinely visual (attribute absence is hard to verify), which the regression residual should expose but could also muddy the headline correlation.
community_default_belief: Negation failure is a joint vision-language reasoning gap requiring multimodal fixes and training data with negated captions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the text tower collapses the negation before fusion, no visual improvement can matter; the failure is inherited upstream and its size is measurable without images.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: embed 50 negated/affirmative phrase pairs in CLIP text space, then check retrieval behavior for the five most and least collapsed pairs.

one_line: Attribute-object binding errors in VLMs grow superlinearly with the number of attributed objects in the scene, following a capacity law of cross-attention rather than a per-object constant error rate.
problem: Binding failures (assigning the red color to the wrong object) are demonstrated with two-object scenes, but how failure scales with scene complexity is unmeasured, leaving deployments without a load limit for attribute-critical tasks.
core_hypothesis: Binding error per object rises with object count following a superlinear curve with a model-specific capacity knee, because attention resources for maintaining object-attribute association are shared and contended, so scene complexity is a quantitative predictor of binding failure and the knee is a comparable model constant.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled scenes with n attributed objects will show per-object binding error flat up to a knee then rising steeply, knee position will vary across models but be stable across content within a model, and shrinking attention capacity (token pruning) will move the knee left predictably.
why_important: It converts binding from a qualitative flaw into a measurable capacity spec (max reliable attributed objects), directly usable in application design and model comparison.
why_possibly_novel: Binding benchmarks exist for small scenes; scaling-law characterization with a capacity-knee constant appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synthetic scenes with 2 to 16 uniquely attributed objects, query attribute-object pairs, fit per-object error versus n curves per model, and test knee stability across two content families.
main_risk: Synthetic scenes may underestimate real-scene binding difficulty; a natural-image validation subset is needed to anchor the law.
community_default_belief: Binding is a fixed per-model weakness with roughly constant error probability per object pair regardless of scene load.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Association maintenance consumes shared attention capacity, and shared-resource systems degrade nonlinearly at load, not at a constant per-item rate.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: colored-shapes scenes at n in {2,4,8,12}, one VLM, plot binding accuracy versus n and look for the knee.

one_line: Increasing input resolution without increasing visual token budget raises VLM hallucination on fine details: per-token information compression, not resolution, is the operative variable for detail fidelity.
problem: Higher resolution is assumed to reduce hallucination by providing more detail, but if the visual token budget is fixed, each token must compress more content, and the effect of compression ratio on hallucination is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Hallucination rate on detail-level questions is governed by pixels-per-visual-token rather than raw resolution, so raising resolution at fixed tokens increases detail hallucination in describable-but-compressed regions, while raising tokens at fixed resolution decreases it, making the compression ratio a design law for VLM configuration.
falsifiable_prediction: Factorial evaluation over resolution and token budget will show hallucination tracking the ratio (iso-ratio configurations matching), with the paradoxical cell (higher resolution, same tokens) showing more detail hallucination than the lower-resolution baseline.
why_important: Teams tune resolution as a quality dial assuming monotone benefit; a compression law would correct configuration practice across every deployed VLM and explain contradictory anecdotes about resolution scaling.
why_possibly_novel: Token-budget ablations exist for accuracy; the compression-ratio law for hallucination specifically, with the paradoxical prediction, appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one open VLM across a resolution-by-token grid on a detail-question benchmark with hallucination scoring, and test iso-ratio matching plus the paradoxical cell.
main_risk: Token merging strategies inside the vision tower differ across models, so the law's form may be architecture-conditional.
community_default_belief: More input resolution monotonically improves VLM detail fidelity and reduces hallucination.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The language model reads tokens, not pixels; if tokens are overloaded, the decoder fills gaps with priors, and higher resolution at fixed tokens increases overload by definition.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: one VLM with configurable input size, fixed token count, detail-QA on 200 images at two resolutions, compare hallucination rates.

one_line: VLMs lean on embedded text as a crutch for perception questions: removing or altering incidental text in images collapses accuracy on questions that ostensibly require only visual understanding.
problem: Benchmark images are full of incidental text (signs, labels, packaging) that leaks answers; reported visual understanding may partly be OCR-plus-reasoning, but text-reliance is never quantified per capability.
core_hypothesis: For a substantial fraction of benchmark items labeled as visual perception, model accuracy drops sharply when embedded text is inpainted away or adversarially altered, and the text-reliance fraction varies by capability category, being highest for fine-grained recognition and scene understanding, revealing inflated capability estimates.
falsifiable_prediction: Text-removed benchmark variants will show accuracy drops far exceeding human drops on the same variants, altered-text variants (wrong labels painted in) will pull answers toward the painted text, and capability rankings between models will reorder once text-reliance is subtracted.
why_important: Capability inflation misleads model selection for text-free deployment domains (nature, industrial interiors, medical), where the OCR crutch is unavailable and true performance is unknown.
why_possibly_novel: Text-shortcut effects appear in isolated probes; a systematic text-reliance decomposition of standard perception benchmarks appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Inpaint incidental text from a sample of a standard VLM benchmark, verify content preservation with human checks, re-evaluate several VLMs, and compute per-capability text-reliance fractions.
main_risk: Inpainting quality issues could depress accuracy for non-text reasons; the altered-text (rather than removed-text) condition controls for this.
community_default_belief: OCR ability is a bonus capability layered on top of genuine visual understanding, not a substitute for it in benchmark performance.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Text is the highest-signal-to-noise feature in any image containing it, and training rewards using it; substitution rather than addition is the efficient learned solution.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: pick 100 benchmark items containing text, paint over the text, re-query one VLM, and compare accuracy drop against a no-text control set.

one_line: VLM performance on an image is predicted by how likely that image's natural description is under web caption style: content whose honest description diverges from alt-text conventions fails regardless of visual difficulty.
problem: Failure analysis focuses on visual attributes of hard images, ignoring that VLM training aligns images to a narrow stylistic register of text, so images whose accurate descriptions are stylistically improbable (geometric, procedural, relational) may fail for text-distribution reasons.
core_hypothesis: The likelihood of an image's ground-truth description under a caption-style language model predicts VLM task accuracy on that image beyond visual difficulty measures, so style-improbable content (dashcam geometry, instrument panels, tables of objects) forms a coherent failure stratum invisible to visual-attribute mining.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-image VLM accuracy on caption-style likelihood will show a significant effect after controlling for visual complexity metrics, and rewriting task prompts toward caption-register phrasing will recover accuracy on the style-improbable stratum but not the control stratum.
why_important: It reframes part of failure mining from image space to text-distribution space, giving a cheap corpus-side predictor of failure and a prompt-side mitigation, both testable without retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is well known; using caption-style likelihood of the scene description as a failure predictor appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score benchmark images' reference descriptions with a caption-corpus language model, evaluate VLMs, and fit accuracy models with and without the style-likelihood covariate; run the phrasing-mitigation arm on the extreme strata.
main_risk: Caption-style likelihood correlates with content rarity, so visual-difficulty controls must be strong to isolate the text-side effect.
community_default_belief: VLM failure on unusual content reflects visual rarity; the text side is a neutral output channel.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Contrastive and captioning objectives only bind images to text that plausibly occurs; content that occurs visually but is rarely captioned faithfully is trained to align with whatever text does occur, which is systematically off-task.
fastest_falsification: One day: rank 500 benchmark images by description likelihood under a caption LM and compare VLM accuracy of the bottom versus top deciles at matched visual complexity.

one_line: VLM visual verification has a phrasing-dependent yes-bias: agreement rates track question-form frequency in training text, so the same visual fact gets different answers under logically equivalent phrasings.
problem: Verification benchmarks use one phrasing per fact, so the measured accuracy confounds visual grounding with the model's phrasing-conditioned response prior, and the size and structure of that prior is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: For fixed visual evidence, the yes/no response distribution shifts systematically across logically equivalent phrasings (positive, negative, tag-question, existential forms), the shift direction follows form-frequency statistics of instruction corpora, and phrasing-marginalized evaluation changes both absolute scores and model rankings on standard verification suites.
falsifiable_prediction: A phrasing battery over identical visual facts will yield response shifts far exceeding sampling noise with a stable direction per form, and ensemble-over-phrasings scoring will reorder some model pairs relative to single-phrasing benchmarks.
why_important: Verification is the backbone of hallucination measurement itself; if the measuring instrument has a phrasing prior, hallucination literature numbers carry a systematic bias of unknown sign.
why_possibly_novel: Yes-bias is noted in VQA history; its quantitative linkage to phrasing-form frequency and its effect on modern hallucination benchmark validity appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct logically equivalent phrasing sets for a verification benchmark sample, evaluate several VLMs, quantify per-form response shifts, and recompute benchmark rankings under phrasing marginalization.
main_risk: Some phrasings subtly change the queried proposition; linguistic review is needed to certify equivalence.
community_default_belief: Modern instruction-tuned VLMs answer verification questions from visual evidence, with phrasing a second-order nuisance.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Instruction tuning optimizes response distributions conditioned on text form; where visual evidence is weak or ambiguous, form-conditioned priors dominate by construction.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: ask one VLM the same 100 visual facts in four equivalent phrasings and measure the spread of yes rates.

one_line: Visual sycophancy is dose-dependent: VLM agreement with false user assertions about an image rises lawfully with the assertion's expressed confidence, quantifying how much visual evidence is worth against social pressure.
problem: Sycophancy is demonstrated with binary contrasts (user asserts versus asks), but the tradeoff curve between assertion strength and visual evidence strength is unmeasured, so deployments cannot bound the risk of user-induced visual errors.
core_hypothesis: Agreement probability with a false visual claim is a smooth increasing function of linguistic assertion strength and a decreasing function of visual evidence strength, and the two combine in a stable, model-specific exchange rate (how much evidence offsets one step of assertiveness), which characterizes deployment risk better than any single sycophancy score.
falsifiable_prediction: A factorial design crossing assertion-strength ladders with evidence-strength ladders will yield monotone response surfaces whose fitted exchange rate is stable across content domains within a model but differs across models and RLHF recipes.
why_important: Interactive deployments (medical second reads, insurance claims review) inject assertive user text routinely; an exchange-rate constant makes the resulting risk computable rather than anecdotal.
why_possibly_novel: Sycophancy is studied in LLMs and noted in VLMs; the quantitative evidence-versus-assertiveness exchange-rate framing appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build image sets with graded evidence for a target fact, cross with assertion phrasings from neutral to insistent, measure agreement surfaces for several VLMs, and fit the exchange-rate model.
main_risk: Assertion strength is hard to scale linguistically in equal steps; validation of the assertiveness ladder with human raters is required.
community_default_belief: Sycophancy is a binary alignment bug largely fixed by newer RLHF, not a lawful tradeoff still present at some exchange rate in every model.
why_that_may_be_wrong: RLHF reweights but does not remove the user-agreement gradient; a reduced but nonzero exchange rate is the expected outcome, invisible to binary probes that only sample one point of the surface.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: one image set, three assertion strengths, one VLM; check whether false-claim agreement rises monotonically with assertiveness.

one_line: VLMs read chart values by interpolating tick labels rather than measuring geometry: continuous-value readout errors quantize toward tick values and gridline positions, revealing symbolic rather than metric chart perception.
problem: Chart QA benchmarks score final answers, obscuring how values are extracted; if models snap to tick labels rather than measuring bar heights or line positions, error structure should be quantized, which no benchmark currently tests.
core_hypothesis: The error distribution of VLM continuous-value chart readouts concentrates at tick and gridline values (quantization), error magnitude scales with inter-tick spacing rather than rendering resolution, and removing tick labels collapses performance to near-chance even when geometry remains fully informative.
falsifiable_prediction: Histogram of readout errors will show mass spikes at tick-aligned values, doubling tick density will roughly halve error independent of resolution, and label-free charts with identical geometry will show a performance collapse disproportionate to the information removed.
why_important: Chart reading is marketed as a core VLM capability for analytics; a symbolic-readout mechanism implies silent large errors whenever data lies between sparse ticks, which is the common case in real dashboards.
why_possibly_novel: Chart benchmarks measure accuracy; the quantization signature analysis identifying the readout mechanism appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render synthetic charts with controlled tick densities, true values placed on and off ticks, and label-free variants; evaluate VLM readouts and analyze error quantization and tick-density scaling.
main_risk: Different chart types (bar, line, scatter) may engage different mechanisms, requiring stratified conclusions.
community_default_belief: VLM chart errors are noisy imprecision that scales down with better resolution and more chart training data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If readout were metric, error would track pixel precision; the quantization prediction distinguishes symbolic interpolation from measurement, and only the latter improves with resolution.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 100 synthetic bar charts with values strictly between ticks; check whether one VLM's answers cluster on the tick values.

one_line: Multi-image VLM prompts exhibit serial-position failure: evidence in middle images is used less than in first or last positions, independent of content, mirroring long-context positional biases in the visual channel.
problem: Multi-image reasoning is benchmarked with position-confounded designs; whether image position in the prompt sequence causally affects evidence usage is untested, though the text-side analog (lost in the middle) is established.
core_hypothesis: For questions answerable from exactly one of n images, accuracy as a function of the evidence image's position will be U-shaped (primacy and recency advantages), the effect will grow with n and with per-image token count, and position randomization will change measured multi-image capability scores for current benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Rotating the evidence image through all positions with content fixed will produce systematic U-shaped accuracy curves across models, and benchmarks re-scored with position marginalization will shift model rankings for at least some pairs.
why_important: Multi-image workflows (document sets, medical series, surveillance timelines) place critical evidence at arbitrary positions; a positional usage bias is a direct deployment hazard and an evaluation confound simultaneously.
why_possibly_novel: Lost-in-the-middle is established for text; a controlled positional causal test for interleaved image sequences appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct n-image prompts where a single image contains the answer, permute its position systematically, evaluate several VLMs at several n, and fit positional accuracy curves.
main_risk: Some architectures compress images asymmetrically by design (early images at lower resolution), which is a mechanism, not a confound, but must be reported per architecture.
community_default_belief: Attention over interleaved image tokens is position-agnostic enough that image order is a stylistic choice without accuracy consequences.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Visual tokens inherit the same positional encoding and attention dynamics that produce text positional biases; there is no mechanism by which images would be exempt.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: five-image prompts, evidence image rotated through positions, one VLM, 100 questions; plot accuracy by position.

one_line: Viewpoint failure maps of detectors and VLMs are predictable from web pose statistics: performance tracks the rendering-estimated frequency of each viewpoint in web imagery, enabling failure forecasting without pose-labeled data.
problem: Rare-viewpoint failure is known qualitatively (top-down bicycles fail), but there is no quantitative bridge from pose frequency statistics to failure probability, so viewpoint risk cannot be forecast for new categories or deployments.
core_hypothesis: Per-viewpoint accuracy for a category is an increasing function of that viewpoint's frequency in web imagery (estimable via pose estimation or rendering-based retrieval), the function's shape is shared across categories within a model, and therefore viewpoint failure maps for unseen categories are predictable from corpus statistics alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Rendering controlled viewpoint sweeps of 3D assets and evaluating recognition will produce accuracy-versus-pose curves that correlate strongly with corpus pose-frequency estimates, and the fitted frequency-to-accuracy function from some categories will predict held-out categories' viewpoint failure maps.
why_important: Robotics and inspection systems encounter uniform viewpoint distributions while models learn photographer-biased ones; a transferable forecasting function converts that mismatch into a computable pre-deployment risk map.
why_possibly_novel: Pose robustness studies exist; the corpus-frequency forecasting function with cross-category transfer appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render viewpoint grids for a set of 3D categories, evaluate detectors and VLMs, estimate web pose frequencies via retrieval against pose-canonical renders, and test the frequency-accuracy regression plus held-out-category transfer.
main_risk: Render-to-real gap could distort absolute accuracies; relative viewpoint structure should survive, but a small real-photo validation set is needed.
community_default_belief: Viewpoint robustness is an emergent property of scale that no longer follows training-frequency structure in large models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Scale reduces but does not equalize exposure; frequency ratios of viewpoints in web data span orders of magnitude, far beyond what emergent invariance has been shown to bridge.
fastest_falsification: One day: viewpoint sweep renders of 10 objects through one detector; correlate per-pose recall with a simple canonical-pose-similarity proxy for web frequency.

one_line: A large share of missed detections in crowded scenes are suppression failures, not recognition failures: the correct box existed before NMS or query deduplication and was deleted by the post-processing stage.
problem: Failure mining operates on final detector outputs, attributing crowd misses to perception, though the pipeline stage responsible (raw predictions versus suppression logic) is never identified case-by-case.
core_hypothesis: Auditing pre-suppression candidate sets will show that for crowded-scene misses, a well-localized correctly-classified candidate existed above a reasonable score in a substantial fraction of cases, so the operative failure is deduplication policy, and this fraction is architecture-dependent (highest for classical NMS, present but different for set-prediction deduplication).
falsifiable_prediction: Stage-attributed failure audits will assign a large, quantifiable share of crowd misses to suppression, oracle-suppression (keeping the best candidate per ground truth) will recover that share exactly, and the recovered share will rank architectures differently than final-output benchmarks do.
why_important: If suppression owns a large failure share, the community's investment balance (backbones and data versus suppression logic) is misallocated, and mined 'hard cases' used for retraining are teaching the wrong lesson since perception already succeeded.
why_possibly_novel: NMS problems in crowds are known; systematic per-instance stage attribution of mined failures and its consequence for failure-mining validity appear unquantified (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several detectors on crowd benchmarks, log pre-suppression candidates, match misses against candidates, compute stage-attribution fractions, and compare oracle-suppression recall recovery across architectures.
main_risk: Defining 'a good candidate existed' requires score and IoU thresholds whose choice affects the headline fraction; sensitivity analysis is mandatory.
community_default_belief: Crowd misses reflect occlusion-limited perception; post-processing is a mature component contributing little to the error budget.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Suppression logic embeds a no-two-objects-overlap prior that crowds violate by definition; the prior deletes correct work product, and final-output evaluation cannot see the deletion.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: one anchor-based detector on a crowd dataset, dump pre-NMS boxes for 100 misses, and count how many misses had a matching pre-NMS candidate.

one_line: DETR-style object queries specialize to spatial-scale niches during training, so scenes whose object layout mismatches the learned query portfolio fail predictably, computable from layout statistics without image content.
problem: Query specialization is documented as an interpretability curiosity, but its failure consequence (a fixed portfolio of location-scale slots that some scene layouts overload) has not been turned into a predictive failure model.
core_hypothesis: The per-scene miss rate of set-prediction detectors is predicted by a mismatch score between the scene's object layout distribution and the model's query specialization map (estimable offline from decoder cross-attention statistics), with overloaded niches producing misses even at low total object counts.
falsifiable_prediction: Scenes constructed to concentrate objects in one query niche will show miss rates far above count-matched dispersed scenes, and a layout-mismatch score computed from ground-truth boxes alone (no pixels) will predict per-scene recall with meaningful correlation across datasets.
why_important: A content-free failure predictor enables triage of incoming imagery before inference and explains a class of dense-scene failures that occlusion-based stories cannot, since the objects need not occlude to overload a niche.
why_possibly_novel: Query specialization analyses exist; converting them into a validated content-free per-scene failure predictor appears novel (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate query specialization maps for public DETR variants, composite count-matched concentrated versus dispersed layouts, measure recall, and validate the mismatch-score regression on natural datasets.
main_risk: Iterative decoder refinement lets queries migrate at inference, potentially blunting niche overload for moderate concentrations; the effect may require extreme layouts to expose.
community_default_belief: Set prediction with Hungarian matching allocates queries flexibly at inference, so layout statistics should not create systematic misses below the query-count ceiling.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training carves stable attractors: matching repeatedly assigns similar layouts to the same queries, and inference-time flexibility is bounded by those learned basins rather than the nominal query count.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: composite scenes with eight objects clustered in one quadrant versus spread out, run one DETR variant, and compare recall at matched visibility.

one_line: Small-object detection relies on context priors more than on object pixels: inpainting the surroundings while preserving the object collapses detection, showing 'small-object failure' is substantially context-prior failure.
problem: Small-object failure is attributed to insufficient object resolution, but detectors may actually be detecting plausible-context-plus-blob; the causal balance between object evidence and context evidence at small scales is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: At small object scales, context manipulation (inpainting or replacing surroundings) changes detection outcomes more than object manipulation (degrading the object itself), and this reliance ratio inverts at a measurable object size, defining the scale below which detectors are effectively context classifiers whose failures track context typicality rather than object visibility.
falsifiable_prediction: Factorial object-versus-context degradation will show context effects dominating below a threshold size, and small objects in atypical contexts will be missed at rates unexplained by visibility while context-typical decoys (object absent, context present) will elicit false positives at the same scale.
why_important: Deployments assume small-object recall improves with sensor resolution; if the binding constraint is context priors, resolution investment is wasted and atypical-context misses (the dangerous ones) persist.
why_possibly_novel: Context effects in detection are classical; the scale-dependent reliance inversion with a measurable threshold appears uncharacterized for modern detectors (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For objects across scales, run object-degraded, context-degraded, and decoy conditions through several detectors, estimate reliance ratios per scale, and locate the inversion threshold.
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts may themselves suppress detection; a compositing-based control (same object pasted into neutral context) is needed to bound artifact effects.
community_default_belief: Small-object failure is a resolution problem, addressed by higher-resolution inputs, feature pyramids, and tiling.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Below some scale the object contributes fewer discriminative bits than its context does; a learner minimizing loss must weight context accordingly, making context reliance the optimal (and brittle) solution.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: paste 50 small objects into typical versus atypical contexts at fixed size and compare detection rates for one detector.

one_line: Fixed score thresholds do not transfer across domains: per-domain optimal thresholds vary enough to reorder failure importance, so much of mined deployed 'failure' is threshold miscalibration rather than model error.
problem: Deployments tune one operating threshold on validation data and hold it fixed; score distributions shift across domains, silently moving the operating point, but failure mining treats the resulting misses and false alarms as model failures.
core_hypothesis: Score distributions shift across deployment domains substantially more than ranking quality degrades, so per-domain threshold recalibration (no retraining) recovers a large fraction of apparent cross-domain failure, and mined failure sets before versus after recalibration differ enough to change remediation priorities.
falsifiable_prediction: Across domain-shift benchmarks, the gap between fixed-threshold and per-domain-optimal-threshold operating performance will constitute a large share of the total cross-domain degradation, and failure taxonomies mined at fixed thresholds will contain a quantifiable stratum that vanishes under recalibrated thresholds.
why_important: It separates the cheap correctable component of deployment failure (a one-parameter fix) from the genuine generalization gap, preventing failure-mining pipelines from feeding threshold artifacts into expensive retraining loops.
why_possibly_novel: Threshold sensitivity is known operationally; quantifying its share of mined failure corpora and its distortion of failure taxonomies appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate detectors across a domain suite at fixed versus per-domain-optimal thresholds, decompose degradation into ranking versus thresholding components, and diff the mined failure sets under both regimes.
main_risk: Per-domain optimal thresholds require labeled deployment data to compute, so the practical claim needs an unsupervised threshold-adaptation arm to be actionable.
community_default_belief: Cross-domain performance drops measure model generalization; the operating threshold is a fixed property of the product configuration.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A monotone shift of the score distribution changes nothing about what the model knows but everything about what a fixed threshold reports; conflating the two overstates model failure by the thresholding share.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: one detector on two domains; compare fixed-threshold F1 against per-domain best-F1 and note the gap share.

one_line: Detection recall has cliffs at the aspect-ratio boundaries of learned box priors: elongated objects fail not gradually but at sharp prior-set boundaries that differ per architecture and are invisible in category-level metrics.
problem: Aspect-ratio robustness is untested as a continuous variable; anchors, query embeddings, and regression ranges all impose soft shape priors whose failure boundaries nobody maps.
core_hypothesis: Per-object recall as a function of ground-truth box aspect ratio shows steep declines at architecture-specific boundary values traceable to prior sets (anchor ratios, query statistics, regression target normalization), so extreme-shape failures (ladders, poles, trains head-on, cables) are structured cliffs, and the cliff locations are predictable from the architecture configuration without any evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: Aspect-ratio-conditioned recall curves will show inflection points aligned with configured anchor ratios for anchor-based detectors and with training-set shape percentiles for set-prediction detectors, and modifying the prior set will move the cliffs to the predicted new locations.
why_important: Extreme aspect ratios are enriched in infrastructure and safety content; knowing cliff locations from configuration enables pre-deployment risk statements without exhaustive testing.
why_possibly_novel: Anchor design is studied for average accuracy; failure-cliff mapping as a function of continuous shape with configuration-based prediction appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite or render objects across a controlled aspect-ratio sweep at fixed area, measure recall curves for several detector families, and align inflections with their configured priors, then re-train one detector with shifted priors to confirm cliff movement.
main_risk: Natural-image evaluation confounds aspect ratio with category; synthetic sweeps avoid this but need a natural-data validation slice.
community_default_belief: Modern detectors regress boxes freely enough that aspect ratio is a smooth, minor difficulty factor.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Regression is learned within the support of training shape statistics and initialized around priors; outside the support, extrapolation fails abruptly rather than smoothly.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: render one object stretched through ratios 1:1 to 20:1 at fixed area in real backgrounds and plot single-detector recall versus ratio.

one_line: Recall for adjacent object pairs collapses at an architecture-specific inter-object IoU threshold: the collapse point is a signature of the deduplication mechanism (NMS versus set prediction), not of the data.
problem: Pairwise proximity failure is folded into crowd metrics; treating pair recall as a function of the ground-truth overlap between neighbors would expose mechanism-specific transition points, but this curve is never measured.
core_hypothesis: Plotting pair-recall (both objects found) against inter-object box IoU yields a sigmoid collapse whose midpoint and slope are stable per architecture family across datasets, with NMS-based models collapsing at their suppression threshold and set-prediction models collapsing later but more steeply, making the curve a fingerprint of deduplication logic measurable from behavior alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Collapse midpoints will cluster by deduplication mechanism across models and datasets, midpoints for NMS models will track their configured IoU threshold when it is changed, and the curve will predict per-scene pair misses better than object count or density does.
why_important: It replaces vague crowd difficulty with a one-parameter behavioral constant per model that deployments can measure cheaply and use to select architectures for proximity-critical tasks (retail shelves, pedestrians in groups, medical cell pairs).
why_possibly_novel: NMS thresholds are obviously known internally; the behavioral pair-recall curve as a cross-dataset architecture signature and its comparative statics appear undocumented (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite controlled object pairs across an IoU sweep in varied scenes, measure pair-recall curves for anchor-based, NMS-free, and set-prediction detectors, and test midpoint clustering plus threshold-tracking.
main_risk: Class-dependent NMS settings and soft-NMS variants blur the single-midpoint story into a family of curves needing per-configuration treatment.
community_default_belief: Proximity failure is a data problem (occlusion, crowding) that better models reduce continuously, rather than a mechanism constant with a measurable transition.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Deduplication logic applies a hard geometric rule independent of appearance; hard rules produce sharp behavioral transitions that data-side explanations cannot generate.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: composite pairs at IoU {0.1,...,0.7} and plot pair recall for one NMS detector against its known suppression threshold.

one_line: For out-of-vocabulary objects, class-agnostic localization survives while classification collapses: most 'unknown object' failures are label-space failures, and mining should separate the two channels.
problem: Open-world failure reports conflate not-seeing an object with not-naming it; if boxes and masks for unknown categories are largely intact, the failure lives in the label head, which changes both mitigation and how failures should be counted.
core_hypothesis: On categories absent from training vocabularies, objectness and localization quality of modern detectors degrade mildly while classification fails near-totally, so channel-separated failure accounting will reattribute the majority of open-world misses from perception to labeling, and downstream mitigations (label-space expansion, retrieval-based naming) will recover much of the loss without touching the visual pathway.
falsifiable_prediction: Class-agnostic evaluation on unseen categories will show localization recall within a modest gap of seen categories while classification accuracy collapses, and attaching a retrieval-based naming head to the frozen detector will recover a large share of end-task performance.
why_important: It redirects open-world robustness work from expensive visual retraining toward cheap label-space mechanisms and corrects failure-mining pipelines that currently over-count perception failures.
why_possibly_novel: Open-vocabulary detection exists as a method area; the failure-accounting decomposition claim (most open-world failure is label-space) with its mining consequence appears unquantified across modern detectors (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Hold out category groups from a detector's vocabulary, evaluate class-agnostic localization versus classification on held-out instances, and measure recovery from a frozen-backbone retrieval naming head.
main_risk: Truly novel visual categories (unlike held-out common ones) may also degrade localization; the held-out design must include visually atypical groups to bound this.
community_default_belief: Unknown-category failure means the detector does not perceive the object, requiring visual retraining on new data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Objectness is learned as a category-general signal and transfers broadly; the label head is the only component with a hard vocabulary boundary, so the collapse should localize there.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: evaluate one detector class-agnostically on a dataset with categories outside its vocabulary and compare localization recall against its in-vocabulary recall.

one_line: Objects touching image borders are missed at rates far exceeding occlusion-matched interior objects because crop augmentation teaches 'truncated equals ignorable': a training-policy failure masquerading as an occlusion problem.
problem: Border truncation is treated as ordinary occlusion, but random-crop augmentation systematically creates truncated instances whose labels are dropped or clipped by policy, injecting a consistent anti-supervision signal for border-touching objects that nobody audits.
core_hypothesis: Detection recall conditioned on border contact will show a penalty beyond visibility-matched interior occlusion, the penalty size will vary with the training stack's crop-labeling policy (label-drop thresholds), and retraining with truncation-preserving labeling will shrink the border penalty without affecting interior performance.
falsifiable_prediction: Visibility-matched comparisons will show a significant border-specific recall deficit across standard detectors, deficits will differ across training stacks in proportion to their label-drop aggressiveness, and the policy-controlled retrain will close the gap.
why_important: Border objects are disproportionately important in egocentric and driving views (objects entering the frame are the newest hazards), so a trained-in border blindness is a direct safety issue with a data-policy fix.
why_possibly_novel: Crop augmentation policies are engineering details; their causal contribution to border-conditioned failure appears unmeasured (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build visibility-matched border versus interior test pairs by controlled cropping of full scenes, evaluate standard detectors, then retrain one detector under different truncation-labeling policies and compare border penalties.
main_risk: Visibility matching between border truncation and interior occlusion is subtle (occluders provide context that borders do not), requiring careful stimulus construction.
community_default_belief: Border misses are ordinary partial-visibility failures, already covered by occlusion robustness efforts.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Occlusion leaves an occluder as evidence and keeps labels; crop policies delete labels for truncated instances, making the border case uniquely anti-supervised rather than merely harder.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: compare recall for objects at 50 percent visibility via border truncation versus 50 percent visibility via interior occlusion for one detector.

one_line: Topology errors (fragmentation, false merges) in segmentation are invisible to IoU at the sizes that matter, so failure mining ranked by IoU systematically excludes the failure class that breaks downstream connectivity-dependent applications.
problem: Vessels, roads, wires, and neurites are consumed downstream as graphs, where a one-pixel break changes connectivity; IoU-based mining scores such masks as near-perfect, so the mined failure distribution is censored exactly where applications are most sensitive.
core_hypothesis: The correlation between IoU and topology correctness (Betti number errors, connectivity of skeletons) approaches zero for thin-structure content, so IoU-ranked failure mining recovers only a small fraction of topology failures, and topology-aware mining surfaces a disjoint, application-critical failure set with different visual causes (low-contrast gaps, crossings, junctions).
falsifiable_prediction: On thin-structure datasets, the overlap between worst-by-IoU and worst-by-topology case sets will be small, topology failures will concentrate at junctions and low-contrast segments rather than where IoU errors concentrate, and retraining on IoU-mined cases will leave topology error rates nearly unchanged.
why_important: Failure-mining pipelines feed retraining; if the metric censors a failure class, the improvement loop is structurally blind to it, and medical or mapping products inherit unfixable connectivity errors while dashboards show progress.
why_possibly_novel: Topology-aware losses exist; the claim that metric choice censors mined failure distributions, with the disjoint-sets prediction, appears unexamined as a failure-mining methodology result (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On vessel and road datasets, mine worst cases by IoU and by topology metrics separately, measure set overlap and cause composition, and run the retraining arms to compare which failure class each mining regime fixes.
main_risk: Topology metrics are sensitive to ground-truth skeletonization choices, requiring robust metric implementations before the comparison is credible.
community_default_belief: High-IoU models are good models; residual topology issues are a niche concern handled by specialized losses when needed.
why_that_may_be_wrong: IoU weights pixels equally while connectivity weights a few pixels infinitely; two metrics with such different weightings must disagree, and mining inherits the blindness of whichever one it uses.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: on one vessel dataset, rank 200 predictions by IoU and by a connectivity metric and report the rank correlation and worst-decile overlap.

one_line: Segmenters systematically fill holes: masks for genus-nonzero objects (donuts, handles, meshes, frames) close their holes because training corpora are overwhelmingly genus-zero, making shape genus a predictor of a distinct failure class.
problem: Mask quality is evaluated without regard to topology class of the object; if models carry a strong genus-zero prior, an entire family of everyday objects fails in a characteristic way (hole filling) that boundary and IoU metrics under-report.
core_hypothesis: Predicted masks exhibit a measurable bias toward filling enclosed background regions, the bias strength scales inversely with hole size and with the rarity of genus-nonzero masks in training data, and hole-filling errors persist even when the hole's background content is high-contrast and unambiguous, indicating a learned topological prior rather than a local appearance failure.
falsifiable_prediction: On a genus-stratified test set, hole-preservation rates will be far below boundary-quality-matched expectations, will decrease with hole-to-object area ratio, and will improve substantially after fine-tuning on synthetic genus-rich supervision without any architecture change.
why_important: Grasp planning, part inspection, and image editing all consume mask topology; a systematic genus prior means these applications fail on a predictable object family and the fix is data-side and cheap.
why_possibly_novel: Hole-filling is an occasional anecdote; genus as a quantitative failure covariate with a training-composition mechanism appears unstudied (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble genus-stratified objects (real photos plus renders), measure hole-preservation across public segmenters, estimate genus statistics of training corpora from their annotations, and run the synthetic-supervision fine-tune arm.
main_risk: Interactive models may resolve holes with additional negative clicks, so single-prompt and multi-prompt regimes must be reported separately.
community_default_belief: Hole errors are local appearance failures on low-contrast interior regions, not evidence of a topological prior.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The prediction that high-contrast holes still get filled distinguishes a learned prior from appearance failure; only the prior explains contrast-independent filling.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: prompt SAM on 50 donut-like objects with clear backgrounds through their holes and count hole-preserving masks.

one_line: SAM-style part-whole granularity choice is intrinsically unstable: trivially small input perturbations flip the same prompt between part and whole masks, and the instability is a fixed property of ambiguity handling, not resolvable by prompt engineering.
problem: Promptable segmentation embraces ambiguity via multi-mask outputs, but production use selects one mask; how stable that selection is under nuisance perturbation (one-pixel shifts, tiny noise, JPEG requantization) is unmeasured and may constitute a first-order reliability failure.
core_hypothesis: For prompts near part-whole ambiguity, the selected-mask granularity flips under perturbations far below perceptual relevance, flip probability is predicted by the score margin between candidate masks, and no prompt-side strategy (offsets, multi-point) eliminates the unstable region because it reflects a decision boundary intrinsic to the ambiguity representation.
falsifiable_prediction: Perturbation sweeps will show granularity flip rates far above those of category decisions at matched confidence margins, flip probability will follow the candidate score margin, and prompt-engineering strategies will relocate but not shrink the total measure of the unstable region.
why_important: Labeling pipelines and interactive tools assume prompt determinism up to noise; granularity instability corrupts datasets silently (mixed part/whole labels for the same concept) and breaks reproducibility of downstream evaluations.
why_possibly_novel: SAM ambiguity is a design feature; its nuisance-perturbation instability profile and the conservation-of-instability claim appear untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample prompts across objects with part structure, apply calibrated nuisance perturbations, measure granularity flip rates versus candidate margins, and evaluate three prompt-engineering strategies for total unstable-region measure.
main_risk: Granularity must be operationalized (mask area ratios, containment relations), and edge cases blur the part-whole dichotomy.
community_default_belief: Multi-mask output plus the quality score handles ambiguity adequately; users experiencing flips are prompting badly.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Ambiguity means near-equal scores by definition, and near-equal scores plus any input sensitivity guarantees flips; the failure is structural, so blaming prompting misdiagnoses it.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 100 part-ambiguous prompts, add one-pixel translations, and measure how often the top-scoring mask changes granularity.

one_line: Segmenters have a measurable behavioral boundary between stuff and things that mismatches human intuition: stuff regions with countable texture elements (waves, clouds, foliage clumps) trigger thing-like fragmentation failures.
problem: The stuff-things division is a dataset convention, but models internalize their own version of it; where the model's implicit boundary sits, and how it fails when texture becomes countable, is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: As stuff textures increase in element discreteness (from smooth water to distinct waves), segmentation behavior transitions from coherent regions to fragmented pseudo-instances at a measurable discreteness threshold, the threshold differs across models and from human judgments, and the transition zone concentrates a distinctive failure class (region shattering) invisible in standard per-class scores.
falsifiable_prediction: A discreteness-graded stimulus continuum will reveal sigmoid-like fragmentation onset per model, thresholds will differ across models trained with different stuff conventions, and human annotators will place their region-versus-objects boundary at a systematically different point than the models.
why_important: Aerial, maritime, and environmental monitoring live inside the transition zone (water states, vegetation, cloud fields); knowing each model's fragmentation threshold predicts where its outputs stop being usable as regions.
why_possibly_novel: Stuff-things is discussed as ontology; the behavioral threshold measurement and its mismatch with human judgment appear unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build or curate a texture-discreteness continuum (natural images ranked by element separability plus synthetic controls), run panoptic and promptable segmenters, quantify fragmentation versus discreteness, and collect human boundary judgments for comparison.
main_risk: Discreteness must be operationalized independently of model behavior (e.g., via human counts or spectral statistics) to avoid circularity.
community_default_belief: Stuff-things handling follows dataset definitions closely; failures at the boundary are rare annotation edge cases rather than a structured behavioral transition.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models interpolate between contradictory conventions across datasets and content, and interpolation across a categorical boundary produces exactly the graded behavioral transition the hypothesis predicts.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: run a panoptic segmenter on a calm-to-stormy water image series and measure region fragment counts versus a wave-discreteness proxy.

one_line: Segmenters misassign reflected and refracted content systematically by physical surface type: mirror content becomes objects, glass transmission merges with occluders, following a taxonomy predictable from surface optics rather than appearance.
problem: Reflection failures are reported as isolated bloopers; whether they follow a lawful taxonomy indexed by surface physics (specular mirror, glossy, transmissive, refractive) is untested, so no risk model exists for reflective environments.
core_hypothesis: Assignment errors (segmenting virtual content as real, merging transmitted with reflected layers) occur at rates and in directions determined by surface type and viewing geometry, forming a stable confusion structure across models, because training annotation conventions for each surface type are themselves systematically different and internally inconsistent.
