falsifiable_prediction: A surface-typed evaluation set will show error direction (virtual-as-real versus real-as-virtual) switching predictably with surface type, consistent across model families, and annotation audits of training sets will reveal matching convention inconsistencies per surface type.
why_important: Retail, indoor robotics, and driving (glass facades, wet roads) are reflection-dense; a physics-indexed failure taxonomy converts sporadic bloopers into a computable coverage requirement for data collection.
why_possibly_novel: Mirror and glass segmentation exist as niche tasks; the cross-model confusion-structure claim tied to annotation-convention audits appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate scenes across surface types with layer-resolved ground truth (what is real, reflected, transmitted), evaluate general segmenters, tabulate directional confusion rates, and audit training-set annotations for the same surface types.
main_risk: Layer-resolved ground truth is labor-intensive; renders can substitute but need a real-photo validation subset.
community_default_belief: Reflection errors are unstructured hard cases requiring generic robustness improvements or niche specialist models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The optics of each surface type produce consistent image evidence, and annotation conventions per type are consistent-ly inconsistent; both forces are systematic, so the failures they generate cannot be unstructured.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: run one segmenter on 50 mirror scenes and 50 glass-storefront scenes and compare the direction of layer misassignment.

one_line: Whether masks include attached shadows follows per-dataset annotation policy, and models trained on mixtures produce class-dependent shadow inclusion, creating an irreducible cross-dataset error floor that is pure convention conflict.
problem: Shadow handling is unspecified in most annotation guidelines and settled inconsistently per dataset and class; the resulting supervision conflict and its share of measured segmentation error are unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Model shadow-inclusion behavior is a learned mixture over training conventions, varying by class and context in ways traceable to source datasets, so a quantifiable fraction of cross-dataset boundary and region error is convention conflict that no model improvement can remove without a convention standard, and this fraction sets a floor on cross-dataset benchmark scores.
falsifiable_prediction: Shadow-inclusion audits of model outputs will match weighted training-set conventions per class, re-scoring cross-dataset evaluations with shadow-agnostic metrics (excluding shadow-ambiguous pixels) will recover a measurable score fraction, and models will disagree with each other on shadow pixels far more than on object pixels.
why_important: It quantifies how much of the segmentation leaderboard gap is metaphysics (what counts as the object) rather than perception, informing both benchmark design and deployment expectations in shadow-heavy domains (aerial, outdoor robotics).
why_possibly_novel: Annotation inconsistency is a known nuisance; isolating attached shadows as a measurable convention-conflict component with a floor estimate appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate shadow-ambiguous pixel sets on cross-dataset samples, audit model outputs for inclusion behavior against training provenance, and re-score benchmarks with shadow-aware exclusion zones.
main_risk: Distinguishing attached shadows from dark object parts requires careful annotation, though disagreement zones can be defined operationally by annotator splits.
community_default_belief: Shadow handling is a negligible pixel fraction; segmentation error differences reflect model quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Attached shadows border every outdoor object and concentrate exactly at boundaries where modern metrics focus, so their pixel share understates their metric share by a large factor.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: for 100 outdoor instances, measure inter-model disagreement rates on shadow-adjacent pixels versus matched object-interior pixels.

one_line: The same texture is classified as different categories depending on apparent scale, and segmenters lack scale anchoring: aerial and macro imagery elicits systematic class flips governed by patch-level scale ambiguity.
problem: Semantic classes are implicitly scale-indexed (moss versus forest, sand versus gravel field), but models receive no metric scale; how class decisions behave under scale ambiguity, and where they flip, is uncharacterized for modern segmenters.
core_hypothesis: Per-region class posterior of segmenters is a function of apparent (pixel) scale with sharp class-flip boundaries, flips follow the training-set scale distribution per class rather than any scene-consistent scale inference, and injecting weak metric-scale cues (known object, GSD metadata encoding) removes a large share of flips, demonstrating the failure is missing scale anchoring rather than texture ambiguity.
falsifiable_prediction: Zooming continuously into fixed scenes will produce reproducible class-flip boundaries at model-specific apparent scales, flip locations will correlate with class scale statistics in training data, and scale-cue injection will suppress flips substantially more than resolution increases do.
why_important: Satellite, drone, microscopy, and macro domains all operate at nonstandard scales; a scale-flip map per model tells deployments at which ground-sample distances the outputs become untrustworthy.
why_possibly_novel: Scale robustness is studied as size invariance for objects; class-flip mapping for texture semantics under scale ambiguity with the anchoring intervention appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build continuous zoom stacks (real aerial pyramids plus macro series), run segmenters, locate flip boundaries, correlate with per-class training scale statistics, and test the scale-cue injection arm.
main_risk: Zoom changes both scale and context; context-controlled crops are needed to isolate the scale variable.
community_default_belief: Scale invariance from augmentation covers texture semantics; class decisions follow visual evidence rather than an unanchored scale guess.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Scale augmentation teaches invariance for objects with shape anchors, but pure textures have no shape anchor, leaving class choice to a prior over apparent scale that augmentation actually randomizes into incoherence.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: zoom sequence over forest aerial imagery through a segmenter; record the apparent scale at which labels flip between vegetation classes.

one_line: Interactive segmentation has a diverging failure regime: for a characterizable case subset, additional corrective clicks make masks worse (oscillation), and click-response stability is a hidden quality dimension uncorrelated with first-click accuracy.
problem: Interactive models are benchmarked by clicks-to-target-IoU averages, which assume monotone improvement; the existence, size, and structure of a non-convergent regime where correction backfires is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of instances enters oscillatory or divergent correction dynamics (mask quality decreasing or cycling with added clicks), membership is predictable from early-interaction signals (mask change magnitude per click), and the diverging subset differs across models even at matched average click efficiency, making stability an independent selection criterion.
falsifiable_prediction: Long-horizon interaction traces will show non-monotone quality trajectories for a stable minority of instances, a two-feature early-warning predictor will forecast divergence, and model rankings by average clicks-to-IoU will disagree with rankings by divergence rate.
why_important: Human annotation budgets assume correction converges; diverging cases silently consume multiplied labeling cost and inject worst-quality masks precisely on hard instances that matter for downstream training.
why_possibly_novel: Interactive segmentation metrics average over interactions; the dynamical-systems framing (convergent versus oscillatory regimes) and stability ranking appear new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate standard click protocols to 20+ clicks on large datasets across interactive models, classify per-instance trajectories, fit early-warning predictors, and compare model rankings under efficiency versus stability metrics.
main_risk: Click simulation strategy affects dynamics; results need at least two established simulation protocols plus a small human-in-the-loop validation.
community_default_belief: More corrective clicks monotonically improve masks; average click-efficiency captures interactive quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Each click re-conditions a nonlinear model on a changed input; nonlinear feedback systems generically possess non-convergent regimes, and averages are exactly the statistic that hides them.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: run 15-click simulated corrections on 300 instances for one model and count instances whose best mask occurred before the final click.

one_line: Population-level smooth degradation under corruption is an aggregation artifact: per-instance failure is cliff-like, with each image having a sharp corruption threshold, which changes the correct mitigation strategy entirely.
problem: Corruption benchmarks report accuracy versus severity as smooth curves, and robustness methods are designed for gradual degradation; whether individual instances actually degrade gradually or flip abruptly at instance-specific thresholds is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: For most corruption families, per-instance prediction-versus-severity trajectories are step functions (correct until an instance-specific threshold, then persistently wrong), the threshold distribution across instances generates the smooth population curve, and threshold location is predictable from instance-level features, so robustness should be framed as threshold-shifting rather than curve-flattening.
falsifiable_prediction: Dense severity sweeps per instance will show step-like transitions for a large majority of instances (transition width much smaller than the severity range), the population curve will be recoverable as the threshold CDF, and instance thresholds will be stable across corruption seeds.
why_important: If failure is threshold-like, average-severity training is misallocated: what matters is moving each instance's cliff past the deployment severity, and monitoring should track distance-to-cliff, a fundamentally different quantity than average robustness.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption robustness is a mature area, but the per-instance trajectory shape question and the threshold-CDF decomposition appear unasked (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep corruption severity in fine steps for individual images across several corruption types and models, classify trajectory shapes, and test population-curve recovery from the threshold distribution.
main_risk: Some corruption families (noise) may show genuinely stochastic flip regions rather than clean steps, requiring a trajectory taxonomy rather than a binary claim.
community_default_belief: Robustness curves reflect gradual per-instance degradation, so improving average robustness improves all instances proportionally.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Classification is a discrete readout of a continuous drift toward a boundary; the readout mathematically produces steps per instance, and only the population mixture looks smooth.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: 50 images, one corruption at 30 severity levels, one classifier; plot per-image correctness trajectories and count step-like versus gradual.

one_line: In-the-wild failure budgets are dominated by interactions between individually-handled factors (rain plus night, blur plus crowd), not by any single factor, making single-axis robustness benchmarks structurally unable to predict deployment failure.
problem: Robustness is evaluated one nuisance axis at a time, implicitly assuming additive effects; deployment failures may live mostly in interaction terms that no single-axis benchmark can surface, but the interaction share of the failure budget is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: A factorial decomposition of failure rates over nuisance-factor combinations will show pairwise and higher-order interaction terms contributing a larger share of total failure than main effects for realistic factor ranges, and models ranked identically on single-axis benchmarks will diverge widely on interaction cells, explaining why benchmark robustness fails to predict field reliability.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled factorial evaluations will yield super-additive failure in a large fraction of factor pairs, interaction magnitude will grow with model accuracy on main effects (as easy failures are removed), and single-axis scores will predict factorial-cell performance poorly.
why_important: The community's robustness scoreboard could be optimizing main effects while the deployment failure mass migrates into interactions, a measurable form of benchmark myopia with direct consequences for safety cases.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption compositions appear occasionally; the failure-budget decomposition framing with the super-additivity growth claim appears unquantified (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a factorial evaluation over 4-6 realistic nuisance factors (illumination, weather, blur, density, scale) via controlled capture or high-fidelity synthesis, evaluate several models, and estimate a failure-rate ANOVA decomposition.
main_risk: Full factorial realism is expensive; synthesis fidelity for factor combinations must be validated against a small real-capture matched set.
community_default_belief: Single-axis robustness scores compose approximately additively, so covering each axis in benchmarks covers deployment.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Each factor consumes shared signal margin (contrast, resolution, context); consuming margin from multiple sides is multiplicative in effect near the margin's floor, which is exactly where hard deployments operate.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: evaluate one detector on night, rain, and night-plus-rain subsets of an existing driving dataset and test failure super-additivity.

one_line: Robustness to a nuisance factor measured along one variation axis does not predict robustness along correlated real-world axes of the same factor: robustness is anisotropic, and benchmark axes are misaligned with natural variation.
problem: Benchmarks operationalize each nuisance (lighting, blur, weather) with one synthetic generator, then generalize conclusions to the factor as a whole; whether robustness transfers across different physical realizations of the same nominal factor is untested.
core_hypothesis: For nuisance factors with multiple physical realizations (lighting: exposure versus spectrum versus direction; blur: motion versus defocus versus atmospheric), model robustness varies strongly across realizations, cross-realization correlation of per-model robustness is weak, and synthetic benchmark realizations sit systematically off the natural realization manifold, so benchmark-certified robustness fails to transfer to the field realization mix.
falsifiable_prediction: A realization-stratified evaluation will show per-model robustness rankings reordering across realizations of the same factor, and distance between benchmark realizations and natural ones (measured on paired real captures) will predict the transfer gap.
why_important: Certification and procurement rely on benchmark robustness labels; anisotropy means those labels are realization-specific fine print, and the field needs realization-resolved reporting to be meaningful.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic-versus-real corruption gaps are noted for specific cases; the general anisotropy framing with cross-realization ranking instability appears unconsolidated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For lighting and blur, assemble three realizations each (synthetic transform, physical capture variation, optical variation), evaluate a model panel, and quantify cross-realization rank correlations plus the benchmark-to-natural transfer gap.
main_risk: Equating severity across realizations is nontrivial; severity must be normalized by human performance or information-theoretic proxies.
community_default_belief: A model robust to a benchmark's version of a nuisance factor is robust to that factor in the field, up to severity matching.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Different realizations of one nominal factor destroy different image statistics, and models overfit the statistics of the specific generator they were hardened against; the factor label is a human abstraction the model never saw.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: compare a model panel's robustness rankings under synthetic gamma-darkening versus real low-light captures of matched difficulty.

one_line: Vision models carry camera-model-specific failure biases: ISP pipelines (denoising, sharpening, tone mapping) leave fingerprints that shift model behavior, and a camera-fingerprint term explains failures currently attributed to content.
problem: Failure analyses index errors by content, place, and condition, never by capture device; if per-device ISP signatures systematically shift model outputs, a hidden covariate contaminates every failure taxonomy built from mixed-device data.
core_hypothesis: Per-device error rates on content-matched imagery differ significantly, the differences are attributable to ISP processing choices rather than optics (reprocessing RAW from one device through another device's ISP style transfers the error pattern), and adding a device-fingerprint covariate to failure models absorbs variance previously assigned to content categories.
falsifiable_prediction: Content-matched cross-device evaluation will show reproducible per-device accuracy offsets, RAW reprocessing swaps will move errors in the predicted direction, and failure-mining clusters recomputed with device covariates will dissolve some previously content-labeled clusters.
why_important: Fleets mix camera models constantly (phones, vehicles, drones); a device-level failure covariate matters for procurement, dataset curation, and for cleaning the failure-mining literature of a systematic confound.
why_possibly_novel: Device fingerprints are known in forensics; their causal effect on FM failure structure and failure-taxonomy validity appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture content-matched scenes with multiple devices (plus RAW where possible), evaluate standard models, estimate device effects with mixed models, and run the RAW-reprocessing transfer arm.
main_risk: Perfect content matching across devices is hard outdoors; lab scenes and tripod-swapped captures bound the confound.
community_default_belief: ISP variation is within the noise floor of model robustness; content and conditions explain failures.
why_that_may_be_wrong: ISPs apply learned, content-adaptive transforms tuned per vendor, and models are sensitive to exactly the statistics ISPs alter (noise texture, edge profiles, local contrast).
fastest_falsification: Half a day: photograph one scene set with two phone models, run one detector, and compare per-device error patterns on matched objects.

one_line: Mined hard-case corpora cluster more by capture metadata (time, place, device, pipeline) than by visual content, so much of what failure mining calls content difficulty is recoverable provenance structure.
problem: Failure mining outputs are interpreted as content-defined weakness maps, but nobody measures how much of the mined structure is explained by non-content metadata, which would redirect fixes from modeling to acquisition governance.
core_hypothesis: Clustering mined failure sets in metadata space will explain a substantial share of failure variance (higher than content-cluster explanations for a nontrivial fraction of clusters), metadata-matched control sampling will dissolve those clusters, and remediation targeted at the metadata stratum (pipeline fixes, acquisition changes) will outperform content-targeted retraining on them.
falsifiable_prediction: Variance-decomposition of failure indicators over content versus metadata factors will assign significant unique variance to metadata, and dissolving-versus-persisting cluster classification under metadata-matched resampling will be reproducible across mining runs.
why_important: Every failure-driven data flywheel (mine, label, retrain) assumes content causation; a large metadata share means flywheels are partly retraining on acquisition artifacts, an expensive and correctable mistake.
why_possibly_novel: Metadata confounds are acknowledged in dataset papers; quantifying their share inside mined failure corpora and testing remediation routing appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a deployment-scale mined failure set with rich metadata, fit variance decompositions and cluster analyses in both spaces, and run a small remediation comparison on one metadata-dominated cluster.
main_risk: Metadata and content correlate naturally (night images contain night content); careful causal analysis (matching, reweighting) is needed to assign unique variance.
community_default_belief: Mined failure clusters reveal what the model cannot see, i.e., content weaknesses to be fixed with more data of that content.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Mining selects on the model's output errors, which respond to everything in the pipeline, not just content; selection concentrates whatever systematic non-content variation exists, making metadata enrichment the expected outcome, not the exception.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: for any public hard-case set with EXIF, test whether failure membership is predictable from metadata alone above chance.

one_line: Failures concentrate in temporal transition regimes (rain onset, dusk, tunnel exits) rather than steady adverse states, because static datasets sample states, not transitions, leaving transition dynamics unlearned.
problem: Adverse-condition robustness is trained and measured on steady-state imagery (fully rainy, fully dark); real systems traverse transitions where mixed statistics (partially wet roads, mixed lighting, adapting exposure) occur, and these mixtures may be off-manifold for models despite both endpoints being covered.
core_hypothesis: Failure rates during condition transitions exceed rates in either adjacent steady state at matched nominal difficulty, the excess is largest for transitions creating statistically novel mixtures rather than interpolations (wet-but-bright, headlights-in-daylight), and adding transition-sampled data reduces the excess more efficiently than adding more steady-state data.
falsifiable_prediction: Time-indexed evaluation across natural transitions will show failure-rate peaks localized to transition windows, peaks will persist after controlling for average scene difficulty, and steady-state-only training augmentation will fail to remove the peaks while transition-sampled fine-tuning removes them.
why_important: Autonomous systems make their worst decisions during environmental transitions when timely perception matters most; a transition-localized failure law identifies a data-collection blind spot with an actionable fix.
why_possibly_novel: Adverse-condition robustness is heavily studied at steady state; transition-regime failure localization and the mixture-novelty mechanism appear unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect or curate continuous sequences spanning transitions (dashcam dusk sets, rain onsets), evaluate detectors and segmenters with time-resolved failure rates, control for difficulty, and run the transition-data fine-tune arm.
main_risk: Difficulty control across a transition is tricky since the transition may be genuinely harder; human performance on the same frames provides the difficulty baseline.
community_default_belief: Covering the endpoints of a condition (clear and rainy) covers the path between them, since intermediate states are visual interpolations.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Physical transitions are not pixel interpolations: wet asphalt under sunlight, auto-exposure hunting, and mixed light temperatures create statistics absent from both endpoints, so endpoint coverage says nothing about the path.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: time-resolved detection error on dashcam dusk sequences, testing for an error peak between day and night plateaus.

one_line: Sensor-saturated pixels (highlight clipping, shadow crush) damage predictions superlinearly to their area because normalization and attention propagate clipping artifacts globally, making clipped fraction a strong hidden failure covariate.
problem: Clipping is universal in real captures (sky, headlights, windows) and absent in curated training imagery at the same rates; the functional relationship between clipped-pixel fraction and model failure is unmeasured, though normalization layers give it a mechanism to act globally.
core_hypothesis: Failure probability rises superlinearly with clipped-pixel fraction, the effect extends to predictions about unclipped regions (global leakage through normalization statistics and attention), and pre-inference clipping-aware treatment (masking, inpainting, statistics correction) recovers accuracy on unclipped content, demonstrating leakage rather than information loss as the mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: Error on objects far from clipped regions will still correlate with the image's clipped fraction, controlled clipping insertion (synthetic saturation of irrelevant regions) will degrade predictions about untouched regions, and statistics-corrected inference will remove most of the remote degradation.
why_important: Clipping is uncontrolled and everywhere in deployment (HDR scenes, night driving with light sources); if it acts globally, a large silent failure covariate is missing from every robustness analysis.
why_possibly_novel: Exposure robustness is studied as local information loss; the global-leakage mechanism via normalization and its superlinear law appear untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert synthetic saturation patches of controlled area into task-irrelevant regions across datasets, measure remote-region prediction degradation versus clipped fraction for several architectures, and test statistics-correction recovery.
main_risk: Synthetic saturation must mimic sensor clipping (hard ceiling plus demosaic effects) or the effect may be under- or over-stated relative to real captures.
community_default_belief: Clipping destroys information only where it occurs; models are unaffected in the rest of the image.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Normalization layers compute global statistics and attention mixes tokens globally, so a large anomalous flat region mathematically alters computation everywhere, and clipped regions are maximal anomalies.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: paste saturated white patches covering 5-20 percent of background in 100 images and measure detection accuracy changes on unmodified foreground objects.

one_line: Sim-to-real and real-to-sim failure is asymmetric per model, and the asymmetry direction reveals the model's feature reliance profile (texture-dependent versus geometry-dependent), providing a diagnostic no symmetric-gap analysis captures.
problem: The domain gap between synthetic and real imagery is measured as a symmetric distance, but transfer failure need not be symmetric; the direction and size of asymmetry per model is unmeasured and potentially diagnostic of internal feature reliance.
core_hypothesis: For matched content, per-model transfer degradation differs by direction (real-trained on sim versus sim-trained on real), texture-reliant models suffer more in the real-to-sim direction (missing natural texture statistics) while geometry-reliant models transfer more symmetrically, so the measured asymmetry index correlates with independent texture-bias measures and predicts which robustness interventions will help which model.
falsifiable_prediction: Transfer matrices across model panels will show stable, model-specific asymmetries, asymmetry indices will correlate with established texture-bias metrics, and texture-randomization training will reduce asymmetry specifically for the texture-reliant group.
why_important: Synthetic data pipelines are scaling rapidly; knowing each model's asymmetry profile tells teams whether their synthetic investments will transfer, and the index provides a cheap feature-reliance probe requiring no interpretability tooling.
why_possibly_novel: Domain gap studies quantify symmetric gaps; the directional-asymmetry-as-diagnostic framing appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or gather models on paired sim and real datasets of matched content, evaluate the full transfer matrix, compute asymmetry indices, and correlate with texture-bias measurements plus the texture-randomization intervention.
main_risk: Matched-content sim-real pairs are scarce; digital-twin datasets or careful scene replication is required for clean matrices.
community_default_belief: The sim-real gap is a symmetric distance to be minimized; direction of transfer is irrelevant to understanding it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Distributions differ in which statistics they lack, not just how far apart they are; a model reliant on statistics present in one domain and absent in the other fails directionally, and symmetry would be the coincidence, not the rule.
fastest_falsification: One day: evaluate one real-trained and one sim-trained detector on both domains of an existing sim-real paired dataset and compare directional degradation.

one_line: Most FM failures are linearly predictable from the model's own frozen features before the task head runs: failures are not surprises to the representation, only to the decision layer, enabling near-zero-cost failure prediction.
problem: Failure prediction is treated as requiring auxiliary models, OOD detectors, or ensembles; whether the FM's own representation already linearly encodes upcoming failure is a simpler question nobody has answered cleanly.
core_hypothesis: A linear probe on frozen FM features predicts per-input task failure substantially above chance across tasks and shifts, prediction transfers across task heads sharing the backbone (failure is encoded in the representation, not the head), and the probe's failures-it-cannot-predict form a small, structurally distinct residual (genuine ambiguity) rather than a random subset.
falsifiable_prediction: Frozen-feature linear probes will achieve strong failure-prediction performance on held-out distributions without access to labels at probe-application time, probes trained against one head will transfer to other heads above chance, and the unpredictable residual will be enriched in human-ambiguous cases.
why_important: If failure is linearly legible in features, every deployment can add a near-free failure gate, and the interesting scientific split becomes representation-legible versus representation-illegible failures, a new taxonomy axis.
why_possibly_novel: Confidence-based and OOD-based failure prediction are mature; the systematic claim that linear feature probes suffice and transfer across heads appears unconsolidated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several FM-plus-head combinations, train linear failure probes on frozen features over one distribution, evaluate prediction on shifted distributions and alternate heads, and audit the unpredictable residual.
main_risk: Probe training requires failure labels from some distribution, and transfer may degrade under shifts that alter the failure mechanism itself.
community_default_belief: Failure prediction needs dedicated uncertainty machinery; raw features do not contain accessible foreknowledge of errors.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Failures are driven by feature-space conditions (low margin, off-manifold position, shortcut activation) that are themselves feature-space-measurable; the head discards exactly the information needed to see them coming.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: train a logistic probe on CLIP features to predict a classifier's errors on one dataset and test it on a shifted variant.

one_line: Per-instance loss-landscape sharpness at inference predicts which failures are fixable by fine-tuning and which persist: sharp failures resist repair and incur collateral damage, giving failure mining a repairability dimension.
problem: Failure mining treats all mined cases as equally worth retraining on, but some failures may sit in sharp regions of the loss landscape where local repair is impossible without moving other predictions, and no repairability signal exists in current pipelines.
core_hypothesis: A cheap per-instance sharpness proxy (loss sensitivity to small weight perturbations) computed at mining time predicts post-fine-tune repair success and collateral damage, sharp failures will be enriched in convention conflicts and label noise (where the target itself is inconsistent), and triaging mining outputs by repairability improves the retraining cost-benefit measurably.
falsifiable_prediction: Repair outcomes after standard fine-tuning will correlate with pre-computed sharpness, the sharp stratum will show both lower repair rates and higher collateral damage, and repairability-triaged retraining will outperform untriaged retraining at fixed budget on overall accuracy.
why_important: Retraining loops consume the bulk of applied-vision budgets; a pre-hoc repairability signal converts failure mining from a list of complaints into an actionable, prioritized work queue.
why_possibly_novel: Sharpness is studied for generalization at the model level; per-instance sharpness as a failure-repairability predictor for mining triage appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine failures for a classifier and detector, compute per-instance sharpness proxies, run controlled fine-tuning arms, and measure repair and collateral outcomes against the sharpness prediction.
main_risk: Cheap sharpness proxies may correlate poorly with true landscape geometry; two or three proxy variants should be compared before concluding.
community_default_belief: Any mined failure is a training opportunity; more hard cases in the fine-tune set is monotonically better.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the target for a case conflicts with the model's globally consistent solution (bad label, convention conflict), gradient pressure on it must damage neighbors; such cases are anti-training data, and sharpness may be their signature.
fastest_falsification: One day: fine-tune one model on 200 mined failures, compare repair success between the top and bottom sharpness quartiles computed beforehand.

one_line: Prediction inconsistency under imperceptible input jitter (sub-pixel shifts, quantization dither) marks failures better than confidence does, and the two signals disagree on a structured case subset where jitter is right and confidence is wrong.
problem: Confidence is the default failure signal despite known miscalibration; local input-space stability is almost free to measure, but its failure-detection power relative to confidence, and the structure of their disagreement, is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: A jitter-inconsistency score (prediction variance under a handful of imperceptible input perturbations) detects failures with higher precision-recall than max-confidence for boundary-proximal errors, the confidence-versus-jitter disagreement set is dominated by confidently-wrong shortcut cases (where both fail) and ambiguous cases (where jitter wins), and combining both signals approaches the practical ceiling of training-free failure detection.
falsifiable_prediction: Across models and datasets, jitter-inconsistency will beat max-confidence on failure-detection metrics for a majority of settings, disagreement-set audits will show the predicted composition, and the two-signal combination will dominate each alone.
why_important: Training-free failure detection is the only option for black-box deployments; establishing the cheap jitter signal's superiority and limits would immediately upgrade monitoring practice.
why_possibly_novel: Perturbation consistency appears inside methods (TTA, randomized smoothing); a head-to-head failure-detection characterization against confidence with disagreement-structure analysis appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement jitter batteries for classifiers, detectors, and segmenters, compute failure-detection metrics against max-confidence on matched benchmarks, and audit disagreement sets.
main_risk: Jitter sensitivity varies by architecture (anti-aliased versus not), so the ranking may be architecture-conditional rather than universal.
community_default_belief: Confidence, possibly calibrated, is the practical failure signal; input-perturbation methods add cost without qualitative benefit.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Confidence measures distance to a learned boundary in feature space, while jitter measures the boundary's local geometry in input space; the second contains information the first mathematically cannot, particularly about brittle correct-looking predictions.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: for one classifier on one dataset, compare failure-detection AUROC of max-softmax versus prediction-flip rate under five one-pixel shifts.

one_line: Confidence-based hard-example mining recovers a biased sliver of the true failure distribution: it oversamples ambiguity failures, misses confident systematic failures, and thereby steers improvement loops away from the most dangerous errors.
problem: The mining stage of data flywheels almost universally selects by low confidence or high loss, quietly defining 'failure' as 'diffident failure'; how the mined distribution differs from the true failure distribution is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Comparing exhaustively-labeled failure sets against confidence-mined subsets will show systematic composition bias (under-representation of high-confidence errors by large factors), retraining on confidence-mined data will improve diffident errors while leaving confident-error rates flat or worse, and mining by alternative signals (disagreement with cheap heuristics, jitter inconsistency, cross-model conflict) will recover complementary failure strata.
falsifiable_prediction: The confident-error stratum's share in mined sets will be far below its share in exhaustive audits, longitudinal flywheel iterations will show diverging trends between diffident and confident error rates, and multi-signal mining will measurably rebalance the mined composition.
why_important: Data flywheels are the main applied improvement mechanism in industry; a structural sampling bias in their input stage means sustained investment systematically hardens models against the wrong failure class.
why_possibly_novel: Active-learning sampling bias is studied for label efficiency; its consequence as failure-class steering in deployed mining loops appears unarticulated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Exhaustively label errors on a deployment-like stream, compare composition against confidence-mined subsets, and run two flywheel iterations with confidence-only versus multi-signal mining, tracking per-stratum error rates.
main_risk: Exhaustive labeling at meaningful scale is expensive; a stratified sampling estimator can substitute but adds statistical machinery.
community_default_belief: Low-confidence mining finds the model's failures; more mined data equals targeted improvement on weaknesses.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Low confidence finds where the model knows it struggles; systematic failures are definitionally where it does not know, so the selector is anti-correlated with the most valuable targets.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: on a labeled benchmark, compute what fraction of a model's errors fall above the confidence threshold that a standard mining policy would use, i.e., invisible to mining.

one_line: VLM verbalized confidence is generated from linguistic properties of its own draft answer rather than visual evidence: manipulating answer phrasing changes stated confidence while visual input stays fixed.
problem: Applications increasingly ask VLMs to self-rate certainty about visual claims, assuming the rating reflects perceptual evidence; if the rating is a post-hoc function of answer text style, self-assessment is theater with a mechanism that can be exposed.
core_hypothesis: Verbalized confidence correlates more strongly with linguistic features of the emitted answer (fluency, specificity, answer length, hedging vocabulary availability) than with measured visual evidence strength, and interventions that alter the answer's linguistic frame (forcing specific formats, prefilling partial answers) shift stated confidence at fixed images, while visual-evidence interventions at fixed answer frames shift it far less than normative amounts.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressions will show answer-text features dominating visual-evidence features in explaining stated confidence, prefill manipulations will move confidence substantially at fixed input, and evidence-degradation ladders will move it sublinearly relative to actual accuracy changes.
why_important: Medical, legal, and moderation workflows are being designed around VLM self-rated certainty; demonstrating its post-hoc linguistic origin would force redesign toward external verification signals.
why_possibly_novel: Verbalized calibration is studied for LLM factuality; the mechanism test separating visual-evidence input from answer-linguistics input in VLMs appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a factorial design crossing visual evidence strength with forced answer framings on visual QA items, collect stated confidences, and fit variance decompositions; add prefill-intervention arms.
main_risk: Instruction-tuned models may resist framing manipulations inconsistently, requiring several manipulation techniques for robustness.
community_default_belief: VLM self-rated confidence, while imperfect, primarily tracks the strength of perceptual evidence for the answer.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Confidence tokens are generated by the same next-token machinery as everything else, conditioned most strongly on the immediately preceding text (the answer itself); the architecture offers no privileged channel from visual evidence to the confidence statement.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: same 100 visual questions, prefill confident-style versus hedged-style answer openings, and compare stated confidence distributions at fixed images.

one_line: Failure taxonomies produced by automated error-clustering tools are unstable under reruns, seeds, and embedding choices: the taxonomies describe the mining pipeline more than the model's failure structure.
problem: Slice-discovery and failure-clustering tools output named failure modes that drive engineering decisions, but the reproducibility of those taxonomies under pipeline perturbation has never been systematically audited.
core_hypothesis: Rerunning standard slice-discovery pipelines with perturbed seeds, embedding backbones, or clustering hyperparameters will produce taxonomies with low structural agreement (cluster matching scores near permutation baselines for many slices), the stable core will be small and coarse, and human teams shown taxonomies from different runs will make materially different remediation decisions, demonstrating that taxonomy instability propagates into engineering waste.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-run cluster agreement will fall far below within-run bootstrap agreement, stability will improve only for the largest coarse slices, and remediation choices elicited from practitioners will diverge across taxonomies of the same underlying failure set.
why_important: The field is operationalizing failure understanding through these tools; if outputs are pipeline artifacts, both research conclusions about model weaknesses and industrial remediation roadmaps inherit unmeasured noise.
why_possibly_novel: Slice discovery methods report discovered slices; systematic instability audits with decision-impact measurement appear absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run several public slice-discovery tools repeatedly with controlled perturbations on fixed model-dataset pairs, compute taxonomy agreement statistics, and run a small practitioner study on remediation divergence.
main_risk: Some instability is benign relabeling of the same structure; agreement metrics must operate on case memberships, not names, to avoid overstating the problem.
community_default_belief: Automated slice discovery reveals real, reproducible failure structure that teams can safely build remediation plans on.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Clustering high-dimensional weak signals is notoriously initialization- and metric-dependent, and failure sets are small samples of rare events, the worst case for stable clustering; stability was assumed, never audited.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: run one slice-discovery tool five times with different seeds on one model-dataset pair and compute pairwise slice-membership overlap.

one_line: Fixing mined failures by fine-tuning damages a predictable collateral set of previously-correct cases, and the repair-damage exchange follows a measurable locality law in feature space, defining a conservation-like constraint on cheap fixes.
problem: Targeted fine-tuning on failures is standard practice with regression testing as the only safeguard; whether collateral damage is random or lawfully concentrated near repairs in representation space is unknown, so damage cannot be predicted or budgeted.
core_hypothesis: Post-repair regressions concentrate in feature-space neighborhoods of the repaired cases with damage probability decaying with representational distance, the decay profile is stable per architecture and fine-tuning method (defining a repair kernel), and total repair-minus-damage is approximately invariant across fine-tuning hyperparameters for fixed data, implying a budget that can be estimated before committing to a fix.
falsifiable_prediction: Regression cases will be strongly enriched within measured feature radii of repair targets versus matched controls, the estimated repair kernel will predict held-out collateral damage counts, and hyperparameter sweeps will trade repair against damage along an approximately fixed frontier rather than beating it.
why_important: Continuous-deployment vision systems ship weekly fixes; a validated damage-prediction kernel would replace blind regression testing with pre-hoc risk budgeting and reveal when a fix is net-negative before shipping.
why_possibly_novel: Catastrophic forgetting is studied for tasks and domains; a per-case spatial damage law with kernel estimation for failure-repair workflows appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune models on controlled failure batches, log flips on large evaluation pools, fit damage-versus-distance profiles, validate kernel predictions on new batches, and map the repair-damage frontier across hyperparameters.
main_risk: Feature-space distance may be the wrong metric for damage locality; several representation layers and metrics should be compared before rejecting the law.
community_default_belief: With small learning rates and replay data, targeted fixes are essentially free; regressions are rare accidents rather than lawful consequences.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Weight updates that change one decision necessarily move a region of the function, not a point; locality of that region in representation space is the mathematically expected form, making 'rare accidents' the surprising claim, not the law.
fastest_falsification: One day: fine-tune on 50 failures, identify all flipped cases in a 50k pool, and test whether flips concentrate within the nearest-neighbor radii of the 50 targets.

one_line: Which instances a model will fail on at convergence is largely determined early in training: learning-event signatures (forgetting counts, late first-learn epochs) forecast final failure sets long before training ends.
problem: Failure mining happens after deployment, at maximal cost; if final failure membership is legible from early training dynamics, mining could move upstream, but the forecast horizon and accuracy are unmeasured for modern vision training.
core_hypothesis: Per-instance training dynamics in the first fraction of training (forgetting events, first-learn time, loss oscillation) predict final-model failure membership substantially above chance, prediction transfers to held-out data via a dynamics-trained probe on input features, and the early-determined failure fraction is enriched in data-borne causes (label conflict, rare compositions) versus late-emerging failures that track optimization noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Probes on early-training dynamics will forecast converged-model failures with strong precision at moderate recall, forecast quality will saturate well before mid-training, and the early-predictable stratum will show the predicted cause enrichment under audit.
why_important: Moving failure discovery from post-deployment to early training collapses the cost of the mine-fix loop and gives data teams a triage signal (fix labels, add coverage) while training is still running.
why_possibly_novel: Example difficulty and forgetting statistics exist for curriculum research; their use as converged-failure forecasters with transfer probes in vision FMs appears unconsolidated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument training runs of mid-scale vision models to log per-instance dynamics, train forecast probes at several checkpoints, evaluate against converged failure sets on train-distribution and shifted evaluations, and audit the early-predictable stratum.
main_risk: Requires training instrumentation access, so the claim cannot be tested on API-only foundation models, limiting scope to reproducible-training settings.
community_default_belief: Final failure sets depend on the whole training trajectory and data order; early dynamics are too noisy to forecast them usefully.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Failures caused by data conflicts and coverage gaps exist independent of trajectory details; training dynamics merely reveal them early, and such causes may dominate mined failure sets.
fastest_falsification: One day with a small model: train on CIFAR-scale data logging per-example dynamics, and test whether epoch-10 forgetting statistics predict epoch-200 errors.

one_line: Frame-to-frame prediction flicker in video segmentation spikes seconds before catastrophic tracking losses: instability is a leading indicator with a usable warning horizon, not just a cosmetic artifact.
problem: Temporal instability of video model outputs is treated as an aesthetic smoothness problem to be filtered away, and catastrophic failures (identity switches, mask collapse) are treated as sudden; whether instability temporally precedes catastrophe is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Catastrophic failure events in video segmentation and tracking are preceded by statistically elevated output instability (mask boundary churn, score oscillation) over a horizon of many frames, the precursor holds after controlling for scene difficulty dynamics, and thresholding the instability signal yields early warnings with operationally useful precision, while temporal smoothing (the standard remedy) destroys the warning signal without reducing catastrophe rates.
falsifiable_prediction: Aligned event studies will show instability rising before failures at rates far above matched non-failure windows, warning precision-recall will beat confidence-based baselines at equal lead time, and smoothed pipelines will show unchanged catastrophe rates with eliminated precursor visibility.
why_important: Video perception failures in robotics and driving are dangerous precisely because they arrive unannounced; a validated free precursor signal converts sudden failures into anticipated ones, and indicts the ubiquitous smoothing practice as safety-negative.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal consistency is optimized as a quality target; its role as a catastrophe precursor with event-study validation appears unstudied (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run video segmenters and trackers on datasets with failure annotations, extract instability time series, perform event-study alignment with difficulty controls, and evaluate warning systems against confidence baselines plus the smoothing ablation.
main_risk: Instability and difficulty co-rise with scene changes; the difficulty-controlled analysis is essential and hard to get right.
community_default_belief: Flicker is cosmetic noise to be smoothed; catastrophic failures stem from discrete events (occlusions, cuts) without accessible precursors.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Catastrophes in dynamical prediction systems typically follow loss of stable tracking equilibria, and oscillation is the canonical signature of equilibrium loss; treating it as cosmetics discards the system's own distress signal.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: on one video-object-segmentation benchmark, compare mask-churn statistics in the three seconds before failure events versus random control windows.

one_line: Motion-blur failure depends on blur direction relative to object contours and text orientation, not just magnitude: benchmarks using uniform-direction blur systematically mis-estimate real-world blur robustness.
problem: Blur robustness is benchmarked with scalar severity levels, ignoring that motion blur is a vector; real blur directions correlate with motion geometry (camera shake versus subject motion), and directional interaction with content structure is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: At fixed blur magnitude, failure rates vary strongly with the angle between blur direction and dominant object contours (blur parallel to critical edges preserves them, perpendicular destroys them), so real-world blur robustness depends on the joint geometry of motion and content, and scalar-severity benchmarks misrank models whose directional profiles differ.
falsifiable_prediction: Directional blur sweeps at fixed magnitude will produce failure-rate variation comparable to a full severity step, per-class directional profiles will follow contour statistics (text and thin structures showing the strongest anisotropy), and two models tied on scalar benchmarks will separate under direction-resolved evaluation.
why_important: Handheld, vehicular, and drone imagery have strongly non-uniform blur direction distributions; robustness certification that ignores direction certifies against the wrong distribution and hides model differences that matter in the field.
why_possibly_novel: Motion blur augmentation and deblurring are mature; direction-content interaction as a failure law with benchmark-validity consequences appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply parameterized directional blur to detection and OCR-bearing datasets at controlled magnitudes, evaluate model panels direction-resolved, and quantify direction-content interaction terms plus ranking changes versus scalar protocols.
main_risk: Synthetic linear blur under-represents real blur trajectories (curved shake paths); a real handheld-capture validation subset is needed.
community_default_belief: Blur severity is the operative variable; direction averages out and can be ignored in robustness evaluation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Blur is a directional low-pass filter and image structures are directional; the interaction is dictated by signal processing, and real motion directions are far from uniformly distributed, so nothing averages out.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: fixed-magnitude blur at 0, 45, 90 degrees on scene-text images through an OCR-capable VLM and compare accuracy across directions.

one_line: A large share of claimed temporal understanding in video models fails the shuffle test: predictions are invariant to frame order or time reversal, exposing single-frame shortcuts behind temporal benchmarks.
problem: Video benchmarks credit models with temporal reasoning when answers are correct, without testing whether the temporal dimension was used; the fraction of benchmark performance attributable to genuinely order-sensitive computation is unknown for modern video FMs.
core_hypothesis: For current video models, a substantial fraction of correct answers on temporal-sounding tasks survives frame shuffling and time reversal, the surviving fraction varies strongly by task category (high for appearance-answerable, low for causal-order questions), and benchmark-level temporal capability scores shrink dramatically under order-sensitivity normalization, reordering model comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: Shuffle and reversal invariance rates will be high on tasks marketed as temporal, invariance will predict which items scale poorly with more frames, and order-sensitivity-normalized scores will change model rankings relative to raw benchmarks.
why_important: Temporal understanding claims drive deployment into monitoring and safety applications where order matters (fall detection, procedure verification); capability inflation from single-frame shortcuts is a direct deployment risk and a benchmark-design indictment.
why_possibly_novel: Shuffle controls appear in individual papers historically; a systematic order-sensitivity audit of modern video FMs with normalized scoring appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate video models on standard temporal benchmarks under original, shuffled, and reversed frame orders, compute per-item and per-category invariance, and publish order-sensitivity-normalized capability scores.
main_risk: Shuffling can break tokenization assumptions in some architectures; implementation must distinguish computational breakage from informational insensitivity.
community_default_belief: Strong scores on temporal benchmarks demonstrate temporal reasoning; frame order sensitivity is implied by task design.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Benchmark questions are constructed by humans who see the temporal structure, but answer keys are often recoverable from appearance priors; models exploit whatever suffices, and nothing in the scoring verifies order usage.
fastest_falsification: Three hours: run one video model on 200 temporal-benchmark items with shuffled frames and report the score retention fraction.

one_line: Tracker failures at occlusions are governed by a model-specific memory horizon: failure probability transitions sharply when occlusion duration exceeds a constant that is independent of object appearance, making occlusion risk computable from geometry alone.
problem: Occlusion robustness of trackers is reported as aggregate scores on datasets with uncontrolled occlusion statistics, so no one knows whether failure is governed by a duration threshold, appearance similarity, or scene complexity, preventing any predictive risk model.
core_hypothesis: Per-event tracking failure probability as a function of occlusion duration is sigmoid with a sharp model-specific midpoint (the memory horizon), the horizon is stable across object categories and appearance at matched re-detection difficulty, and horizon length measured on synthetic occlusions predicts real-world failure rates given deployment occlusion-duration distributions.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled occlusion-duration sweeps will produce sigmoid failure curves with tight midpoint estimates per model, midpoints will vary across architectures (memory-based versus detection-based) but not across content at matched conditions, and convolving measured horizons with deployment occlusion statistics will predict field failure rates.
why_important: A single-constant risk model turns occlusion robustness from a leaderboard number into an engineering quantity: deployments can measure their occlusion-duration distribution and compute expected failure rates before installation.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion handling is a core tracking topic; the duration-threshold constant framing with content-independence and field-prediction validation appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate controlled occlusion events (synthetic compositing and staged captures) sweeping duration, fit per-model sigmoid curves, test content independence, and validate field prediction on an annotated real dataset.
main_risk: Re-appearance context (position predictability during occlusion) matters alongside duration; the design must stratify by motion predictability to keep the horizon interpretable.
community_default_belief: Occlusion failure is a complex function of appearance similarity, distractors, and scene clutter, too entangled for a single-parameter law.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Memory mechanisms decay or drift at rates set by architecture, not content; if memory decay is the binding constraint, duration dominates and the entanglement story confuses secondary modulators with the primary variable.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: composite occluders of controlled duration over tracked objects in existing sequences and plot one tracker's failure rate versus duration.

one_line: Video models fail on high-frame-rate and timelapse footage because the operative variable is motion magnitude per frame, not content: frame-rate mismatch is a hidden distribution shift misdiagnosed as content difficulty.
problem: Web training video clusters near standard frame rates, fixing a narrow distribution of inter-frame motion magnitudes; deployment footage (high-speed, timelapse, variable-rate streams) violates it, but evaluations never condition on effective motion-per-frame.
core_hypothesis: Video model accuracy is a function of inter-frame motion magnitude with a tuned optimum near web-typical values, degrading on both sides (too-small motion starves temporal signals, too-large motion breaks correspondence assumptions), so resampling deployment footage to web-typical motion-per-frame recovers accuracy without any model change, proving the failure is rate mismatch rather than content.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy versus motion-per-frame curves will be non-monotone with an interior optimum consistent across content types, temporally resampling high-fps and timelapse footage toward the optimum will recover a large share of the deficit, and the optimum will track the training corpus's motion statistics across models trained on different corpora.
why_important: Industrial inspection, sports analytics, and surveillance increasingly use non-standard frame rates; a resampling fix and a corpus-statistics predictor would immediately improve deployments and re-attribute a class of mined failures from content to acquisition.
why_possibly_novel: Frame-rate augmentation exists as a trick; the motion-per-frame distribution-shift framing with the interior-optimum prediction and corpus-tracking test appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate video models on fixed content captured or resampled across a wide motion-per-frame range, fit accuracy curves, run the resampling-recovery arm, and compare optima across models with documented training corpora.
main_risk: Resampling introduces its own artifacts (frame interpolation errors, temporal aliasing) that must be bounded with capture-native high-fps ground truth.
community_default_belief: Video models generalize across frame rates since content is unchanged; failures on unusual footage reflect unusual content.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Temporal architectures learn correspondence and motion priors calibrated to the training inter-frame displacement scale; content identity is irrelevant to whether those priors match the input's temporal sampling.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: take one action-recognition model, evaluate the same clips at native rate and subsampled by factors of 2 to 16, and plot accuracy versus effective motion-per-frame.

one_line: Long-video question answering degrades with the timestamp position of evidence independent of content: a visual lost-in-the-middle effect that makes video-length capability claims position-confounded.
problem: Long-video benchmarks report aggregate accuracy versus video length, but evidence position within the video is uncontrolled; if positional usage bias exists, length-capability claims conflate context capacity with positional attention artifacts.
core_hypothesis: For fixed content and fixed video length, accuracy on questions whose evidence occupies a controlled temporal position will vary systematically with that position (strongest at start and end), the positional penalty will grow with video length and token compression aggressiveness, and position-marginalized scoring will materially lower reported long-video capabilities and reorder models.
falsifiable_prediction: Sliding the same evidence clip through positions in padded videos will produce U-shaped accuracy curves, the mid-video penalty will scale with length, and models using different temporal compression schemes will show distinguishable positional profiles predictable from their architecture.
why_important: Long-video understanding is a headline capability race; position-confounded evaluation misleads model selection for applications where critical events occur at arbitrary times (security review, medical procedure audits).
why_possibly_novel: Lost-in-the-middle is established for text; controlled positional causal designs for long-video evidence appear missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct videos by embedding evidence clips at controlled positions within neutral filler of controlled length, evaluate long-video models across the position-length grid, and fit positional penalty models per architecture.
main_risk: Filler content must be verified non-informative and non-distracting, or filler interactions contaminate the positional estimate.
community_default_belief: Long-video accuracy measures temporal capacity; where evidence sits in the video is averaged out by benchmark diversity.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Benchmark evidence positions are not uniformly distributed (edited content front-loads salience), so averaging does not remove the bias, and attention over compressed temporal tokens has the same positional pathologies as text attention.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: embed 50 evidence clips at 10, 50, and 90 percent positions in 20-minute fillers and compare one model's QA accuracy across positions.

one_line: Deployed vision failures arrive in temporal bursts because consecutive inputs share failure-inducing conditions: per-image metrics understate operational risk, and the failure autocorrelation function is the missing deployment statistic.
problem: Evaluation treats inputs as exchangeable and reports marginal failure rates, but deployments consume correlated streams where one failure predicts more; burst structure determines real-world harm (consecutive missed detections) yet is never measured or modeled.
core_hypothesis: Failure indicator time series from deployed streams exhibit strong positive autocorrelation over condition-persistence timescales, burst-adjusted risk metrics (probability of k consecutive failures) exceed IID predictions by orders of magnitude, and the autocorrelation function is predictable from environmental persistence statistics, enabling stream-level risk certification that per-image metrics cannot provide.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured failure autocorrelation on dashcam and surveillance streams will greatly exceed shuffled-baseline levels, k-consecutive-failure frequencies will match a fitted correlated model and violate IID extrapolations, and cross-deployment ACF differences will track condition-persistence differences.
why_important: Safety cases quantify harm via consecutive-failure probabilities (missed pedestrian across n frames); computing them from marginal rates under IID assumptions is the current practice and may be wrong by orders of magnitude in the dangerous direction.
why_possibly_novel: Correlated errors are acknowledged qualitatively in safety engineering; measured failure ACFs for modern vision systems and their integration into evaluation practice appear absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run detectors on continuous annotated streams, extract failure time series, estimate ACFs against shuffled controls, fit burst models, and compare k-failure predictions against IID baselines and against held-out stream measurements.
main_risk: Continuous ground truth is expensive; semi-automatic annotation with human audit of failure windows makes it tractable.
community_default_belief: Per-frame or per-image failure rates, possibly stratified by condition, adequately characterize deployment risk.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Stratification by known conditions captures only the modeled covariates; residual correlation from unmodeled persistent factors (sensor state, scene geometry, weather microstructure) remains and is exactly what bursts are made of.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: run one detector over a labeled driving sequence set, compute failure-run-length distributions, and compare against the shuffled-order distribution.

one_line: Failure mining only sees failures humans can adjudicate: models are never evaluated on inputs where human ground truth is unattainable, and the adjudication boundary silently shapes both training data and claimed capabilities.
problem: Every benchmark and mined failure set requires human-verifiable labels, so inputs where humans cannot agree or cannot know (extreme conditions, ambiguous scenes, beyond-human acuity regimes) are excluded from evaluation entirely, leaving model behavior there unmeasured and unmineable by construction.
core_hypothesis: Model behavior degrades or becomes pathological beyond the human adjudication boundary in ways detectable without full ground truth (via physical consistency checks, instrument cross-validation, or downstream outcome verification), and the excluded regime constitutes a substantial share of deployment inputs for real systems, so capability claims certified inside the boundary systematically overstate deployed reliability.
falsifiable_prediction: Using instrument-verified ground truth that bypasses human labeling (physical measurements, multi-sensor consensus), model performance in the beyond-adjudication regime will fall significantly below extrapolations from the adjudicable regime, and the deployment share of such inputs will be measurable and non-negligible for several application domains.
why_important: The field's entire evidence base has a selection filter nobody accounts for; quantifying behavior past the filter, and the filter's deployment share, would recalibrate reliability claims for every high-stakes vision application.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation ambiguity is studied within labeled data; the systematic exclusion of unadjudicable inputs and instrument-based measurement of model behavior beyond the boundary appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: In one domain with independent instrumentation (e.g., distance measurement versus monocular estimates, laboratory assays versus visual inspection), assemble input sets spanning the adjudication boundary, measure model performance against instrument truth on both sides, and estimate the deployment frequency of beyond-boundary inputs.
main_risk: Instrument ground truth is domain-specific and expensive, restricting initial evidence to a few domains from which generalization must be argued carefully.
community_default_belief: Benchmark distributions cover deployment adequately; inputs humans cannot label are rare edge cases irrelevant to capability measurement.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Deployment samples nature, not what annotators can label; fog, glare, distance, and ambiguity are common in the world, and their systematic exclusion is an artifact of the labeling economy, not of deployment statistics.
fastest_falsification: One day: compare monocular depth model errors against lidar truth stratified by whether human annotators could confidently order the depths, and check for a performance discontinuity at the adjudication boundary.

one_line: Benchmark-targeted training conserves failure mass rather than destroying it: as benchmarks saturate, failures migrate to input regions outside benchmark support, measurable as unchanged failure rates on independently sampled wild distributions.
problem: Benchmark scores improve steadily, and the community reads this as failure reduction; whether total failure probability under natural input distributions declines correspondingly, or merely relocates outside benchmark support, is untested because nobody maintains benchmark-independent evaluation streams.
core_hypothesis: For successive model generations optimized against saturated benchmarks, failure rates measured on continually refreshed, benchmark-disjoint wild samples decline far slower than benchmark gains imply, the divergence grows with benchmark age (a Goodhart drift law), and failure composition on wild samples shifts toward input types structurally absent from benchmark support, demonstrating migration rather than elimination.
falsifiable_prediction: Longitudinal evaluation of model generations on frozen benchmarks versus freshly-sampled wild sets will show diverging trend lines, wild-set failure composition will shift toward benchmark-unrepresented strata over generations, and the divergence will be largest for the most heavily targeted benchmarks.
why_important: If failure mass is conserved under benchmark optimization, the field's progress metrics systematically overstate reliability gains, and deployment surprise is a predictable consequence of the evaluation economy rather than bad luck.
why_possibly_novel: Goodhart effects and benchmark overfitting are discussed; a quantitative conservation-versus-elimination test with refreshed wild sampling across model generations appears unexecuted (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble model generations spanning several years, evaluate all on their era benchmarks plus a protocol-fixed refreshed wild sample (random web and sensor captures with post-hoc labeling), and compare improvement slopes and failure composition drift.
main_risk: Wild sampling must avoid its own drift and leakage into training corpora of newer models; capture-after-training-cutoff protocols mitigate but complicate comparisons.
community_default_belief: Benchmark gains, especially on diverse modern suites, reflect genuine broad reliability improvement that transfers to deployment distributions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Optimization pressure concentrates improvement exactly on measured support; without pressure elsewhere, error mass has no reason to shrink there, and high-dimensional input spaces have unbounded unmeasured regions for it to occupy.
fastest_falsification: One day: evaluate three model generations on one saturated benchmark and on 500 freshly captured never-online photos of matched content, comparing the two improvement slopes.

one_line: Human-assigned failure categories (occlusion, blur, clutter) misidentify causal mechanisms: ablation-based causal attribution disagrees with human failure labels in a large fraction of cases, invalidating remediation plans built on human taxonomies.
problem: Failure review processes have humans tag error causes by looking at images, assuming visible difficulty equals operative cause; the agreement between these intuitive attributions and intervention-based causal tests has never been measured.
core_hypothesis: For a substantial fraction of mined failures, counterfactual interventions (removing the occlusion, deblurring, decluttering via editing) do not flip the prediction, revealing the human-assigned cause was incidental, the true causes being invisible factors (context priors, convention conflicts, pipeline artifacts) that humans cannot see, so remediation targeted by human taxonomy fixes the wrong variable at scale.
falsifiable_prediction: Intervention audits will show low flip rates for human-attributed causes on a large case fraction, flip-rate-validated taxonomies will differ structurally from human taxonomies, and retraining targeted by validated causes will outperform retraining targeted by human labels at matched budget.
why_important: Industrial failure review is built on human cause-tagging; measuring its causal validity, and finding it poor, would redirect failure analysis toward intervention-based tooling and explain why cause-targeted data collection often underdelivers.
why_possibly_novel: Counterfactual editing exists as a technique; using it to audit the causal validity of human failure taxonomies at scale appears novel (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample mined failures with human cause tags, construct intervention edits per tag with modern editing tools plus quality control, measure prediction flip rates, and run the remediation comparison arm on the largest cause categories.
main_risk: Editing artifacts can flip predictions for spurious reasons; edit-quality controls and placebo edits (matched edits on non-attributed factors) are essential.
community_default_belief: Experienced reviewers can identify why a model failed from inspection; human cause taxonomies are reliable inputs to remediation planning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Humans see the image's salient difficulty, but models fail for model reasons (features, priors, pipeline state) that are invisible in the image; the visible-difficulty heuristic is a category error about where causes live.
fastest_falsification: One day: for 50 failures tagged occlusion, inpaint the occluder away and count how many predictions actually flip to correct.

one_line: A measurable share of benchmark failures are cases where ground truth is contested among annotators: model-truth disagreement and annotator-annotator disagreement overlap heavily, and separating them changes model rankings and failure-rate estimates.
problem: Benchmarks ship single-truth labels, so evaluation cannot distinguish model errors on clear cases from disagreements on inherently contested cases; the contested fraction of reported failures, and its effect on rankings, is unquantified for modern vision benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: Re-annotating benchmark samples with multiple independent annotators will show mined model failures strongly enriched in high-disagreement items, scoring only consensus items will change absolute failure rates substantially and reorder some model pairs, and the contested stratum will have distinct visual characteristics allowing cheap contestedness prediction for un-re-annotated benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Failure enrichment in high-disagreement strata will be several-fold, consensus-only scoring will move model rankings for measurable pairs, and a contestedness predictor trained on re-annotated subsets will transfer across benchmarks with useful accuracy.
